{"answer": "
# LPBF Aluminium Alloy Discovery Campaign: Literature Review and Seed Alloy Recipes

## 1. Quantitative Literature Review by Alloy Family

The following comprehensive table summarises the best-documented compositions, measured chemistries, process parameters, and mechanical properties across the alloy families investigated.

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

### Family (a): Al–Mn–Cr–Zr and Al–Mn–Ti–Zr

**Al–Mn–Cr–Zr (Mehta / Chalmers).** Mehta et al. developed a family of Al–Mn–Cr–Zr alloys specifically for LPBF, with compositions determined by ICP-OES at Höganäs AB (pqac-00000024). Alloy C (Al–5.0Mn–0.8Cr–0.6Zr–0.17Fe–0.24Si, measured) was processed on an EOS M100 (170 W, 1500 mm/s, 0.1 mm hatch, 30 µm layers) and later an EOS M290 (370 W, 1300 mm/s, 0.13 mm hatch, 30 µm layers, 100 µm spot), achieving 99.5–99.8% relative density and inherent crack-freedom across a broad DOE window (pqac-00000026, pqac-00000027). As-built tensile properties averaged across XZ/XY orientations were YS 250 MPa, UTS 310 MPa, and 25% elongation; after direct ageing at 648 K for 24 h these rose to YS 350 MPa, UTS 440 MPa, and 8% elongation, with hardness increasing from ~102 to ~130 HV (pqac-00000047).

Alloy F (Al–4.8Mn–0.9Cr–1.1Zr–1.2Mg, measured ICP-OES) introduced both increased Zr (beyond solubility, triggering grain refinement via primary L1₂-Al₃Zr) and Mg for solid-solution strengthening (pqac-00000024, pqac-00000025). It achieved 99.7–99.8% density and was crack-free, in contrast to Alloy E (Al–4.7Mn–0.8Cr–0.7Zr–1.0Mg) which cracked because its lower Zr content was insufficient for heterogeneous nucleation (pqac-00000025). Alloy F as-built: YS 390 MPa, UTS 450 MPa, 17% elongation; after ageing at 648 K for 8 h: YS 500 MPa, UTS 560 MPa, 5% elongation, hardness 132→172 HV (pqac-00000040, pqac-00000047). The Al-HS1 industrial variant of this family was qualified at component level by Arena et al. (2024); after 375 °C/14 h ageing, horizontal specimens achieved YS 356 MPa, UTS 441 MPa, and 10.4% elongation (pqac-00000045).

**Al–Mn–Ti–Zr (Mair et al.).** A novel Al–4.8Mn alloy modified with Ti and Zr was processed at 380 W, 1900 mm/s, 0.1 mm hatch, 30 µm layers on an unheated substrate (pqac-00000002). The as-built alloy achieved 99.9 ± 0.1% density, was crack-free, and had YS 284 ± 3 MPa, UTS 320 ± 1 MPa, and 16.9 ± 0.2% elongation with 108 ± 1 HV10, primarily from Mn supersaturation (3.7 ± 0.5 wt% retained in matrix) and fine-grain strengthening via primary L1₂-Al₃(Ti,Zr) nucleants (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000004).

### Family (b): Al–Mg–Zr (Addalloy)

Griffiths, Croteau, Dunand and coworkers studied Addalloy™ with measured ICP-OES compositions of Al–3.60Mg–1.18Zr (Batch 1) and Al–3.60Mg–1.12Zr (Batch 2) (pqac-00000048, pqac-00000049). Processing was on a Concept Laser M2 (200 W CW, 1070 nm, 90 µm spot) at 200 mm/s, 0.135 mm hatch, and 30–40 µm layers. As-fabricated YS ranged from ~220 MPa (Batch 1, lower Zr) to ~290 MPa (Batch 2, higher Zr) depending on batch and orientation. After peak ageing at 400 °C for 2–8 h, YS reached 345–359 MPa with ~20% elongation (pqac-00000055, pqac-00000048). The strengthening was dominated by coherent 2–5 nm L1₂-Al₃Zr precipitates formed during ageing, with Mg contributing solid-solution hardening.

### Family (c): Al–Fe–Zr (Aheadd CP1)

Pauzon et al. (2022) reported the Constellium Aheadd CP1 alloy with ICP-measured powder composition of Al–1.02Fe–1.05Zr (O 0.098, N <0.005, H 0.0019 wt%) (pqac-00000006). LPBF was performed on an EOS M290 at 370 W, 1400 mm/s, 0.13 mm hatch, 60 µm layers, with 100 °C platform preheating. Relative density exceeded 99.7%. After stress relief at 300 °C/2 h and direct ageing at 400 °C/4 h, the alloy reached YS 310 MPa with thermal conductivity of 180 W/m·K (pqac-00000006, pqac-00000007). The alloy exploits primary Al₃Zr for crack prevention and nanoscale Al₃Zr + Al₁₃Fe₄ precipitation for strengthening.

### Family (d): Al–Mg–Si Eutectic-Type Alloys (without Zr/Sc/Ti grain refiners)

Yang et al. (2023) processed a pseudo-binary Al–9.6Mg–4.9Si alloy (nominally Al–13.3 wt% Mg₂Si) by LPBF at VED 129.6 J/mm³, achieving 99.3% density and as-built YS 439 MPa, UTS 557 MPa, but only 2.9% elongation—far below the 8% target (pqac-00000013). A related Al–5.39Mg–3.08Zn–1.96Si–0.75Mn alloy (measured ICP) processed on a Farsoon FS271M at VED 129.1 J/mm³ achieved 403 MPa YS, 548 MPa UTS, and 6.7% elongation (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000014). These Zr-free, Si-free alloys demonstrate that high-Mg + Si eutectic compositions can reach >400 MPa YS as-built, but ductility and density are on the edge of the campaign requirements.

### Family (e): Modified Al–Si–Mg

The Al–Mg–Si–Zr alloy Al–7Mg–2Si–1.2Zr (nominal) by Yang et al. (2022) was processed at 170 W, 350 mm/s, 0.15 mm hatch, 30 µm layers, 150 °C plate, achieving as-built YS 447.9 ± 3.6 MPa, UTS 493.4 ± 6.7 MPa, and 9.6 ± 1.1% elongation (pqac-00000021, pqac-00000022). After HT2 (high-temperature ageing), YS further increased to 467 ± 1.3 MPa. This alloy requires Zr for grain refinement.

### Family (f): Er as Sc Substitute

Guo et al. (2022) demonstrated Al–Mg–Mn–Er–Zr alloys. The best performer, specimen 3# with measured composition Al–6.40Mg–0.72Mn–0.40Er–1.10Zr (pqac-00000054), was processed at 350 W, 1000 mm/s, 0.13 mm hatch, 30 µm layers (pqac-00000008). As-built: YS 325 ± 4 MPa, UTS 438 ± 3 MPa, 18.0 ± 1.8% elongation. After direct ageing at 375 °C/10 h: YS 440 ± 3 MPa, UTS 520 ± 2 MPa, 15.5 ± 1.0% elongation (pqac-00000051, pqac-00000052). The strengthening mechanism involves Al₃Er primary nucleation followed by Al₃(Er,Zr) core–shell precipitation. **No crack-free Er-bearing alloy without Zr was identified** in the retrieved literature.

**Al–Ni–Er–Zr (Taheri-Mousavi et al.).** The design composition was Al–2.73Ni–3.19Zr–2.33Er (wt%), ultrasonically atomized and LPBF-processed into crack-free specimens (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000016). The alloy exploits sub-micron metastable Al₂₃Ni₆M₄ ternary phases formed during rapid solidification as reservoirs for 1–5 nm coherent L1₂-Al₃(Er,Zr) nanoprecipitates upon ageing at 400 °C/8 h. As-built hardness was 180 HV; after ageing, peak tensile strength reached ~395 MPa, described as ~50% above the benchmark printable Al alloy and comparable to wrought Al 7075 (pqac-00000016). The design is thermally stable through 48 h at 400 °C.

### Family (g): Low-Sc Al–Mg–Sc–Zr and Al–Mn–Sc

Bayoumy et al. (2023) studied an Al–Mn–Sc alloy with measured composition Al–4.58Mn–1.24Mg–0.91Sc–0.42Zr (wt%, converted from at%) (pqac-00000017). Processed on an EOS M290 at 350 W, 1600 mm/s, 0.1 mm hatch, 30 µm layers, with 200 °C platform heating, the alloy achieved >99.5% density. The heated platform triggered in-situ ageing, precipitating 1.5–2 nm Sc-rich nanoclusters at 1.75 × 10²⁴ m⁻³ density, yielding YS 522 MPa with up to 18% elongation—without any post-build heat treatment (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000019). A related Al–3.04Mn–1.60Mg–0.78Sc–0.22Zr alloy (Zhang et al. 2023, measured) processed at large 120 µm layer thickness and heat-treated at 300 °C/5 h achieved YS 472 MPa and ~10% fracture strain (pqac-00000056, pqac-00000057). These results establish that ~0.8 wt% Sc with 0.2–0.4 wt% Zr is sufficient for fully equiaxed grains and excellent properties; reducing Sc below ~0.3 wt% risks incomplete refinement.

---

## 2. Zr-Free Compositions from Available Feedstock Exceeding ~300 MPa YS

The question restricts elements to Al, Si, Mg, Mn, Cr, Zn, Sn, Ti, Fe, Cu, Ni, Sc, and Er (no Zr, Ce, Li, Ag). Among compositions with published LPBF data:

1. **Al–9.6Mg–4.9Si (pseudo-binary Al–Mg₂Si eutectic):** YS 439 MPa, UTS 557 MPa, 2.9% elongation—**fails the ≥8% ductility criterion** (pqac-00000013).
2. **Al–5.39Mg–3.08Zn–1.96Si–0.75Mn (measured):** YS 403 MPa, UTS 548 MPa, 6.7% elongation, 98.9% density—marginal on ductility and density (pqac-00000012).
3. **Standard AlSi10Mg:** As-built YS ~240–270 MPa—**does not reach 300 MPa** (pqac-00000047).
4. **Al–Mn–Cr (Zr-free ternary from the Mehta family):** Projected as-built YS ~200–250 MPa; aged YS may reach ~300 MPa—not directly demonstrated without Zr (pqac-00000023, pqac-00000026).
5. **Al–Mg–Si–Ti (Wen et al. 2024 concept, 0.77% Ti):** UTS 447.8 MPa, elongation 9.1% as-built—promising but Ti is the nucleant former, and the exact composition was not retrieved in full detail.
6. **AlSi11CuMn:** YS ~350 MPa as-built reported in a review (pqac-00000032).

**Ranking by evidence strength:** The Al–Mg–Zn–Si–Mn composition has the strongest single-paper evidence for a Zr-free alloy exceeding 300 MPa, though its elongation and density are borderline. The pseudo-binary Al–Mg₂Si eutectic has the highest YS but fails ductility. Ti-containing Al–Mg–Si–Ti is the most mechanistically promising Zr-free route toward >400 MPa with ≥8% elongation, but requires validation of the specific composition. No Zr-free, Sc-free alloy in the retrieved evidence simultaneously meets YS >300 MPa, elongation ≥8%, and density ≥99.5%.

---

## 3. Microstructure Expectations for the Campaign's Route

The campaign uses ultrasonically atomized powder (D50 ~55–65 µm, cut to 20–63 µm), an Aconity MIDI (400 W-class, ~80 µm spot), and 30–50 µm layers. Key differences from the literature conditions:

**Coarser powder** (D50 ~40 vs. 15–37 µm in references): Coarser powder produces larger inter-particle voids and lower packing density, requiring higher VED to achieve full densification. Literature alloys like Addalloy used D50 14–37 µm (pqac-00000048, pqac-00000049), and CP1 used 60 µm layers with standard fine powder (pqac-00000006). Coarser feedstock may also have different chemistry (less surface oxide per unit mass but possibly different solidification history inside the particles).

**80 µm spot vs. 40–100 µm in references:** The 80 µm spot is similar to the EOS M290 (100 µm) used for most Mehta alloys and Bayoumy's alloy. The cooling rate will be on the order of 10⁵–10⁶ K/s, adequate for Mn/Cr/Mg supersaturation and primary Al₃Zr/Al₃Ti nucleation.

**Critical microstructural features by family:**
- **Al–Mn–Cr:** Success depends on Mn/Cr remaining in supersaturated solid solution (>3 wt% Mn metastably dissolved) (pqac-00000003). The coarser powder should not critically affect this, as supersaturation is determined by melt-pool cooling rate, not powder size.
- **Al–Mg–Si eutectic:** The α-Al/Mg₂Si eutectic spacing controls strength. Coarser powder and potentially lower cooling rate could coarsen the eutectic, reducing YS.
- **Al–Fe–Ni eutectic:** Similar eutectic-spacing sensitivity. The 80 µm spot should provide adequate refinement.
- **Mg loss:** At 810–840 °C atomization and during LPBF, Mg evaporation is significant for alloys with ≥5 wt% Mg. Add 0.5–1.0% excess Mg to the charge and verify by ICP-OES of both powder and printed material.

**25 °C vs. 150–200 °C plate preheat:** An unheated plate increases residual stress and cracking risk but preserves the supersaturated state. For Sc-containing alloys, a 200 °C plate can provide in-situ ageing equivalent to a post-build treatment (pqac-00000018). For Al–Mn–Cr alloys, the ageing window is 350–400 °C, so a 150–200 °C plate should not cause premature precipitation. Using 150–200 °C for initial builds is recommended.

---

## 4. Direct Ageing Schedules and Expected Hardening

| Family | Direct-ageing schedule | Expected Δ | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Al–Mn–Cr–Zr | 375 °C/8–24 h | +40–50 HV; YS +100–110 MPa | No overageing seen through 2544 h at 250 °C; ~12% loss at 350 °C/1054 h (pqac-00000040, pqac-00000047) |
| Al–Mg–Zr (Addalloy) | 400 °C/2–8 h | YS +100–130 MPa | Coarsening-resistant Al₃Zr; 60 h at 400 °C causes ~15% loss (pqac-00000048, pqac-00000055) |
| Al–Fe–Zr (CP1) | 400 °C/4 h | YS → 310 MPa from ~200 as-built | Precipitation of Al₃Zr + Al₁₃Fe₄ raises conductivity simultaneously (pqac-00000006, pqac-00000007) |
| Al–Mg–Mn–Er–Zr | 375 °C/10 h (or 350 °C/25 h, 325 °C/50–100 h) | YS +115 MPa; HV +40 | Al₃(Er,Zr) core–shell precipitation; stable to ~400 °C (pqac-00000051) |
| Scalmalloy-type | 300–350 °C/4–12 h | YS → 460–520 MPa | 200 °C platform heating can partially substitute (pqac-00000038, pqac-00000039, pqac-00000018) |
| AlSi10Mg | 160–170 °C/6 h | Modest YS increase | Coarsening of Si network above ~200 °C **reduces** strength; heated plate at 150–200 °C causes progressive softening (pqac-00000047) |

**Families that lose strength on a heated plate or during stress relief:** AlSi10Mg is most sensitive—holding at 200+ °C coarsens the Si network and reduces as-built UTS. The Al–Mn–Cr system is robust through ~250 °C but loses hardness above 350 °C over long holds.

---

## 5. Recommended Seed Alloys

The following table provides the six mandatory seeds plus three optional compositions, designed for mechanistic diversity, feedstock compatibility, and informativeness for a SAASBO campaign.

<artifact id="artifact-01"/>

### Design Rationale

**Mechanistic diversity.** The six seeds cover: (1) eutectic Si network hardening (AlSi10Mg); (2) Mn/Cr supersaturated solid solution (Zr-free Al–Mn–Cr); (3) eutectic Mg₂Si + Al₃Ti nucleation (Al–Mg–Si–Ti); (4) Mg + Mn + Cr solution strengthening with deliberate cracking-boundary probing (Al–Mn–Cr–Mg); (5) eutectic Al–Fe–Ni intermetallic network (Al–Fe–Ni); (6) Er-based L1₂ precipitation without Zr (Al–Mg–Mn–Er). Each probes a different strengthening mechanism and different elements, maximising SAASBO information content across 15 candidate elements.

**Feedstock compatibility.** Seeds 1–4 and 6 use only elements on hand (Al from 6063/Al-12Si bar, Mg, Mn, Cr, Ti, Si, Er). Seed 5 requires purchasing Fe and Ni (described as quick to buy). The three optional seeds (7–9) all require purchasing Al–10Zr master alloy.

**Meltability.** All six primary seeds have estimated liquidus temperatures below ~700 °C, well within the 1300 °C induction-furnace capacity. The practical concern is not furnace temperature but rather primary intermetallic formation:
- **Al–Mn–Cr:** At ≥5 wt% Mn, the Mn-rich sludge region (Al₆Mn) may form if the melt is held below ~700 °C for extended periods. Rapid melting and immediate pouring into the atomizer is recommended.
- **Ti-containing alloys (Seed 3):** Al₃Ti has a peritectic temperature of ~665 °C. Ti should ideally be added as an Al–5Ti–1B rod or similar master alloy and dissolved at ≥750 °C, though the charge is small enough that dissolution should be rapid.
- **Er-containing alloys (Seed 6):** Al₃Er forms at ~640 °C. With only 0.3 wt% Er and a 350 g charge, dissolution at 810–840 °C should be achievable.

### What Is Known vs. Unknown for Each Seed

**Seed 1 (AlSi10Mg):** Well-established LPBF alloy with hundreds of publications. Expected to print without issue. Known: as-built YS ~230–270 MPa (pqac-00000047). Unknown: exact performance with ultrasonically atomized coarser powder.

**Seed 2 (Zr-free Al–5Mn–0.8Cr):** The ternary without Zr has not been independently published as a tensile specimen—Mehta's Alloy A (Al–4.7Mn, no Cr, no Zr) and Alloy B (Al–0.8Mn–0.14Cr, no Zr) were ternaries tested only for hardness (~80–90 HV) (pqac-00000023). Crack-freedom is expected based on the Scheil design principle, but the ageing response without Zr precipitation hardening is uncertain.

**Seed 3 (Al–5Mg–2Si–0.7Ti):** Inspired by Wen et al.'s Al–Mg–Si–Ti (UTS 447.8 MPa, 9.1% elongation as-built) and Yang et al.'s high-Mg–Si alloys (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000013). The specific composition is *not a direct reproduction* of any single published alloy. Mg₂Si eutectic backfilling + Al₃Ti nucleation is the mechanism being tested.

**Seed 4 (Al–4.7Mn–0.8Cr–1.0Mg):** The closest literature alloy (Mehta Alloy E, with 0.7 wt% Zr) **cracked** (pqac-00000024, pqac-00000025). This seed deliberately probes whether the alloy cracks without Zr, providing essential boundary information for the optimizer.

**Seed 5 (Al–1.5Fe–1.5Ni):** An exploratory eutectic composition. Al–Fe–Ni eutectic alloys have been investigated for thermal stability but tensile data at this composition are sparse in the retrieved evidence. The narrow freezing range should favour printability.

**Seed 6 (Al–5Mg–0.7Mn–0.3Er):** No Zr-free Er alloy was found to be published as crack-free. This is a high-information exploratory seed to determine whether Al₃Er alone provides sufficient nucleation.

**Optional Seed 7 (Mehta Alloy F reproduction):** Directly reproduces the strongest documented result in the Al–Mn–Cr–Zr family: 500/560 MPa YS/UTS (pqac-00000047). Requires Al–10Zr master alloy purchase.

**Optional Seed 8 (Guo Al–6Mg–0.7Mn–0.4Er–1.1Zr):** Reproduces the best Er-bearing result: 440/520 MPa YS/UTS with 15.5% elongation after 375 °C/10 h (pqac-00000051, pqac-00000052). Requires Zr and uses limited Er stock.

**Optional Seed 9 (Low-Sc Al–4Mg–0.3Sc–0.4Zr):** Tests whether 0.3% Sc with 0.4% Zr provides a useful fraction of Scalmalloy performance (~460–520 MPa) (pqac-00000038, pqac-00000039). Requires both Zr and uses limited Sc stock.

### Key DOIs for Principal Sources

- Mehta et al. 2022: 10.1557/s43578-022-00533-1
- Mehta et al. 2023: 10.1016/j.jallcom.2023.171685
- Martucci et al. 2022: 10.3390/met12081387

- Griffiths et al. 2018: 10.1016/j.matchar.2018.03.033
- Griffiths et al. 2020: 10.1016/j.actamat.2020.02.008
- Pauzon et al. 2022: 10.1016/j.scriptamat.2022.114878
- Guo et al. 2022: 10.1016/j.matdes.2022.111064
- Bayoumy et al. 2023: 10.3390/ma16247586
- Zhang et al. 2023: 10.1080/17452759.2023.2250769
- Yang et al. 2022 (Al–Mg–Si–Zr): 10.3390/ma15155089
- Yang et al. 2022 (Al–Mg–Zn–Si): 10.1016/j.msea.2022.143636

state.question:
We must pick the first SIX aluminium alloy compositions (plus three optional extras) for a laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) alloy discovery campaign, and write a complete recipe for each. Please do a deep, quantitative literature review that lets us choose and specify them. Report MEASURED chemistries (ICP/OES of powder or part) rather than nominal ones wherever the paper gives them, and say which is which.

CONTEXT
- Goal: an alloy that is stronger than LPBF AlSi10Mg (as-built yield about 230-300 MPa) without relying on critical minerals, and/or one that approaches Scalmalloy (Al-4.6Mg-0.7Sc-0.3Zr, about 470-520 MPa yield when direct aged) with much less Sc. Strength first; ductility of at least about 8 %; relative density at least 99.5 %; crack-free.
- Powder: made in-house by 40 kHz ultrasonic atomization of 170-350 g charges melted by induction at up to about 1300 C (so far run at 810-840 C), collected under argon. Median size is coarse (D50 roughly 55-65 um), so the LPBF cut will probably be 20-63 um.
- Feedstock on hand: 6063 bar (carries about 0.5 Mg, 0.4 Si, 0.2 Fe), Al-12Si (4047) bar, Mg, Mn, Cr, Zn, Sn, Ti, Si, and small amounts of Sc and Er. Quick to buy: Fe, Cu, Ni. NOT yet on hand and uncertain: Zr (would come as Al-10Zr master alloy), Ce, Li.
- Printer: Aconity MIDI (400 W-class single-mode fibre laser, about 80 um spot), argon, build-plate heating available. Sub-size tensile bars, as-built and direct-aged.
- After the six seeds a sparse-axis-aligned-subspace Bayesian optimizer (SAASBO) picks the remaining runs over about 15 candidate elements, so the seeds should be mechanistically diverse, not six variants of one family.

QUESTIONS
1. For each family below, give the best-documented specific composition(s) and, per paper: measured composition (wt%), powder route and size, LPBF machine, laser power, scan speed, hatch, layer thickness, spot size, plate preheat, volumetric energy density, relative density, cracking observations, as-built and heat-treated yield strength / UTS / elongation (with build orientation and heat treatment), hardness, and the microstructure reported (grain size and morphology, primary and eutectic phases, precipitates, retained solute). Families:
   a. Al-Mn-Cr-Zr (Chalmers group: Mehta, Nyborg, Hryha and co-workers) and Al-Mn-Ti-Zr (Mair et al.), and Zr-free Al-Mn-Cr or Al-Mn-Mg variants.
   b. Al-Mg-Zr (Croteau, Dunand, Seidman et al.; Addalloy) and Al-Mg-Zr-Mn.
   c. Al-Fe-Zr (Constellium Aheadd CP1 type), Al-Fe-Mg-Zr (Li et al. 2025), binary Al-Fe (Qi, Takata, Kimura), Al-Fe-Cr, Al-Fe-Mn, Al-Fe-Cu, Al-Fe-Ni (AlFeNi eutectic) and Al-Fe-V-Si (8009).
   d. Al-Mg-Si eutectic-type alloys with high Mg (Al-Mg2Si pseudo-binary, Magsimal-59-like AlMg5Si2Mn, Fehrmann AlMgty, the Dreano Al-6.7Mg-3Si-1.4Ni-1Zn alloy) that print crack-free WITHOUT Zr, Sc or Ti grain refiners.
   e. Modified Al-Si-Mg: AlSi7Mg0.6 (A357), AlSi10Mg with raised Mg (1-3 wt%), with Mn, Cu, Ni, Er, Zr or Sc additions; Al-Si-Ni and Al-Si-Fe-Mn; which of these beat standard AlSi10Mg as-built or direct-aged, and by how much.
   f. Er as a Sc substitute: Al-Mg-Er-Zr, Al-Mg-Mn-Er-Zr, Al-Er-Zr, Al-Zr-Er-Yb, Al-Ni-Er-Zr (Taheri-Mousavi et al.). Is there any crack-free Er-bearing alloy WITHOUT Zr?
   g. Low-Sc Al-Mg-Sc-Zr (Sc 0.1-0.4 wt%) and low-Sc Al-Mn-Sc; the lowest Sc level that still gives equiaxed, crack-free builds and an ageing response; Sc partially replaced by Zr, Er, Ti or Y.
   h. Al-Ce(-Mg, -Mn, -Ni, -Zr), Al-Ni(-Mn, -Zr, -Sc), Al-Cu-Mn-Zr (ACMZ), Al-Cu-Mg with Ti, Zr or TiB2 (A20X, 2024+Zr), 7xxx with Zr (HRL 7A77) or with Si, and 6061 with Zr or Si.
   i. Ti as the L1_2 / D0_22 former instead of Zr: Al-Ti, Al-Mg-Ti, Al-Mn-Ti, Al-Cu-Ti, Ti-modified 2xxx/7xxx, Al-5Ti-1B (TiB2) inoculated alloys made by melt routes.
2. Zr is not yet on our shelf. Which compositions made ONLY from Al, Si, Mg, Mn, Cr, Zn, Sn, Ti, Fe, Cu, Ni, Sc and Er (no Zr, Ce, Li, Ag) have been printed crack-free by LPBF with as-built or aged yield strength above about 300 MPa? Rank them by evidence.
3. For each of the top candidates, what microstructure should we expect from OUR route (coarser 20-63 um ultrasonically atomized powder, 80 um spot, 30-50 um layers, with 25 C versus 150-200 C plate), and which features decide success (primary Al3Zr/Al3Ti nucleants at the melt-pool boundary, eutectic fraction, Mn/Cr supersaturation, Mg loss)?
4. Direct ageing (no solution treatment) schedules and expected hardening for each family, and which families lose strength on a heated plate or in stress relief.
5. Please do a deep, quantitative literature review that lets us choose and specify them. CONTEXT
- Goal: an alloy that is stronger than LPBF AlSi10Mg (as-built yield about 230-300 MPa) without relying on critical minerals, and/or one that approaches Scalmalloy (Al-4.6Mg-0.7Sc-0.3Zr, about 470-520 MPa yield when direct aged) with much less Sc. *Table: Comparison of leading LPBF aluminium candidates, distinguishing measured chemistry from nominal or proprietary compositions. NR denotes information not reported in the retrieved source.*

### Family (a): Al–Mn–Cr–Zr and Al–Mn–Ti–Zr

**Al–Mn–Cr–Zr (Mehta / Chalmers).** Mehta et al. developed a family of Al–Mn–Cr–Zr alloys specifically for LPBF, with compositions determined by ICP-OES at Höganäs AB (mehta2023advancingnovelalmncrzr pages 1-3). Alloy C (Al–5.0Mn–0.8Cr–0.6Zr–0.17Fe–0.24Si, measured) was processed on an EOS M100 (170 W, 1500 mm/s, 0.1 mm hatch, 30 µm layers) and later an EOS M290 (370 W, 1300 mm/s, 0.13 mm hatch, 30 µm layers, 100 µm spot), achieving 99.5–99.8% relative density and inherent crack-freedom across a broad DOE window (mehta2022al–mn–cr–zrbasedalloystailored pages 3-4, mehta2022al–mn–cr–zrbasedalloystailored pages 4-5). As-built tensile properties averaged across XZ/XY orientations were YS 250 MPa, UTS 310 MPa, and 25% elongation; after direct ageing at 648 K for 24 h these rose to YS 350 MPa, UTS 440 MPa, and 8% elongation, with hardness increasing from ~102 to ~130 HV (mehta2023developmentofhigh pages 66-69).

Alloy F (Al–4.8Mn–0.9Cr–1.1Zr–1.2Mg, measured ICP-OES) introduced both increased Zr (beyond solubility, triggering grain refinement via primary L1₂-Al₃Zr) and Mg for solid-solution strengthening (mehta2023advancingnovelalmncrzr pages 1-3, mehta2023advancingnovelalmncrzr pages 3-5). It achieved 99.7–99.8% density and was crack-free, in contrast to Alloy E (Al–4.7Mn–0.8Cr–0.7Zr–1.0Mg) which cracked because its lower Zr content was insufficient for heterogeneous nucleation (mehta2023advancingnovelalmncrzr pages 3-5). Alloy F as-built: YS 390 MPa, UTS 450 MPa, 17% elongation; after ageing at 648 K for 8 h: YS 500 MPa, UTS 560 MPa, 5% elongation, hardness 132→172 HV (mehta2023advancingnovelalmncrzr pages 9-12, mehta2023developmentofhigh pages 66-69). The Al-HS1 industrial variant of this family was qualified at component level by Arena et al. (2024); after 375 °C/14 h ageing, horizontal specimens achieved YS 356 MPa, UTS 441 MPa, and 10.4% elongation (arena2024novelaluminumalloy pages 6-8).

**Al–Mn–Ti–Zr (Mair et al.).** A novel Al–4.8Mn alloy modified with Ti and Zr was processed at 380 W, 1900 mm/s, 0.1 mm hatch, 30 µm layers on an unheated substrate (mair2022microstructuralfeaturesand pages 1-2). The as-built alloy achieved 99.9 ± 0.1% density, was crack-free, and had YS 284 ± 3 MPa, UTS 320 ± 1 MPa, and 16.9 ± 0.2% elongation with 108 ± 1 HV10, primarily from Mn supersaturation (3.7 ± 0.5 wt% retained in matrix) and fine-grain strengthening via primary L1₂-Al₃(Ti,Zr) nucleants (mair2022microstructuralfeaturesand pages 4-6, mair2022microstructuralfeaturesand pages 7-8).

### Family (b): Al–Mg–Zr (Addalloy)

Griffiths, Croteau, Dunand and coworkers studied Addalloy™ with measured ICP-OES compositions of Al–3.60Mg–1.18Zr (Batch 1) and Al–3.60Mg–1.12Zr (Batch 2) (griffiths2020coarseningandcreep pages 2-3, griffiths2018effectoflaser pages 1-2). Processing was on a Concept Laser M2 (200 W CW, 1070 nm, 90 µm spot) at 200 mm/s, 0.135 mm hatch, and 30–40 µm layers. As-fabricated YS ranged from ~220 MPa (Batch 1, lower Zr) to ~290 MPa (Batch 2, higher Zr) depending on batch and orientation. After peak ageing at 400 °C for 2–8 h, YS reached 345–359 MPa with ~20% elongation (griffiths2020additivemanufacturingof pages 109-114, griffiths2020coarseningandcreep pages 2-3). The strengthening was dominated by coherent 2–5 nm L1₂-Al₃Zr precipitates formed during ageing, with Mg contributing solid-solution hardening.

### Family (c): Al–Fe–Zr (Aheadd CP1)

Pauzon et al. (2022) reported the Constellium Aheadd CP1 alloy with ICP-measured powder composition of Al–1.02Fe–1.05Zr (O 0.098, N <0.005, H 0.0019 wt%) (pauzon2022anovellaser pages 1-4). LPBF was performed on an EOS M290 at 370 W, 1400 mm/s, 0.13 mm hatch, 60 µm layers, with 100 °C platform preheating. Relative density exceeded 99.7%. After stress relief at 300 °C/2 h and direct ageing at 400 °C/4 h, the alloy reached YS 310 MPa with thermal conductivity of 180 W/m·K (pauzon2022anovellaser pages 1-4, pauzon2022anovellaser pages 8-12). The alloy exploits primary Al₃Zr for crack prevention and nanoscale Al₃Zr + Al₁₃Fe₄ precipitation for strengthening.

### Family (d): Al–Mg–Si Eutectic-Type Alloys (without Zr/Sc/Ti grain refiners)

Yang et al. (2023) processed a pseudo-binary Al–9.6Mg–4.9Si alloy (nominally Al–13.3 wt% Mg₂Si) by LPBF at VED 129.6 J/mm³, achieving 99.3% density and as-built YS 439 MPa, UTS 557 MPa, but only 2.9% elongation—far below the 8% target (yang2023microstructureandmechanical pages 1-2). A related Al–5.39Mg–3.08Zn–1.96Si–0.75Mn alloy (measured ICP) processed on a Farsoon FS271M at VED 129.1 J/mm³ achieved 403 MPa YS, 548 MPa UTS, and 6.7% elongation (yang2022developinganovel pages 1-5, yang2022developinganovel pages 18-21). These Zr-free, Si-free alloys demonstrate that high-Mg + Si eutectic compositions can reach >400 MPa YS as-built, but ductility and density are on the edge of the campaign requirements.

### Family (e): Modified Al–Si–Mg

The Al–Mg–Si–Zr alloy Al–7Mg–2Si–1.2Zr (nominal) by Yang et al. (2022) was processed at 170 W, 350 mm/s, 0.15 mm hatch, 30 µm layers, 150 °C plate, achieving as-built YS 447.9 ± 3.6 MPa, UTS 493.4 ± 6.7 MPa, and 9.6 ± 1.1% elongation (yang2022microstructureandmechanical pages 2-4, yang2022microstructureandmechanical pages 1-2). After HT2 (high-temperature ageing), YS further increased to 467 ± 1.3 MPa. This alloy requires Zr for grain refinement.

### Family (f): Er as Sc Substitute

Guo et al. (2022) demonstrated Al–Mg–Mn–Er–Zr alloys. The best performer, specimen 3# with measured composition Al–6.40Mg–0.72Mn–0.40Er–1.10Zr (guo2022microstructureandmechanical pages 2-3), was processed at 350 W, 1000 mm/s, 0.13 mm hatch, 30 µm layers (guo2022microstructureandmechanical pages 1-2). As-built: YS 325 ± 4 MPa, UTS 438 ± 3 MPa, 18.0 ± 1.8% elongation. After direct ageing at 375 °C/10 h: YS 440 ± 3 MPa, UTS 520 ± 2 MPa, 15.5 ± 1.0% elongation (guo2022microstructureandmechanical pages 4-8, guo2022microstructureandmechanical pages 3-4). The strengthening mechanism involves Al₃Er primary nucleation followed by Al₃(Er,Zr) core–shell precipitation. **No crack-free Er-bearing alloy without Zr was identified** in the retrieved literature.

**Al–Ni–Er–Zr (Taheri-Mousavi et al.).** The design composition was Al–2.73Ni–3.19Zr–2.33Er (wt%), ultrasonically atomized and LPBF-processed into crack-free specimens (taheri‐mousavi2026additivelymanufacturablehigh‐strength pages 9-12, taheri‐mousavi2026additivelymanufacturablehigh‐strength pages 12-15). The alloy exploits sub-micron metastable Al₂₃Ni₆M₄ ternary phases formed during rapid solidification as reservoirs for 1–5 nm coherent L1₂-Al₃(Er,Zr) nanoprecipitates upon ageing at 400 °C/8 h. As-built hardness was 180 HV; after ageing, peak tensile strength reached ~395 MPa, described as ~50% above the benchmark printable Al alloy and comparable to wrought Al 7075 (taheri‐mousavi2026additivelymanufacturablehigh‐strength pages 12-15). The design is thermally stable through 48 h at 400 °C.

### Family (g): Low-Sc Al–Mg–Sc–Zr and Al–Mn–Sc

Bayoumy et al. (2023) studied an Al–Mn–Sc alloy with measured composition Al–4.58Mn–1.24Mg–0.91Sc–0.42Zr (wt%, converted from at%) (bayoumy2023effectiveplatformheating pages 2-3). Processed on an EOS M290 at 350 W, 1600 mm/s, 0.1 mm hatch, 30 µm layers, with 200 °C platform heating, the alloy achieved >99.5% density. The heated platform triggered in-situ ageing, precipitating 1.5–2 nm Sc-rich nanoclusters at 1.75 × 10²⁴ m⁻³ density, yielding YS 522 MPa with up to 18% elongation—without any post-build heat treatment (bayoumy2023effectiveplatformheating pages 1-2, bayoumy2023effectiveplatformheating pages 6-8). A related Al–3.04Mn–1.60Mg–0.78Sc–0.22Zr alloy (Zhang et al. 2023, measured) processed at large 120 µm layer thickness and heat-treated at 300 °C/5 h achieved YS 472 MPa and ~10% fracture strain (zhang2023strongandductile pages 1-3, zhang2023strongandductile pages 5-8). These results establish that ~0.8 wt% Sc with 0.2–0.4 wt% Zr is sufficient for fully equiaxed grains and excellent properties; reducing Sc below ~0.3 wt% risks incomplete refinement.

---

## 2. Zr-Free Compositions from Available Feedstock Exceeding ~300 MPa YS

The question restricts elements to Al, Si, Mg, Mn, Cr, Zn, Sn, Ti, Fe, Cu, Ni, Sc, and Er (no Zr, Ce, Li, Ag). Among compositions with published LPBF data:

1. **Al–9.6Mg–4.9Si (pseudo-binary Al–Mg₂Si eutectic):** YS 439 MPa, UTS 557 MPa, 2.9% elongation—**fails the ≥8% ductility criterion** (yang2023microstructureandmechanical pages 1-2).
2. **Al–5.39Mg–3.08Zn–1.96Si–0.75Mn (measured):** YS 403 MPa, UTS 548 MPa, 6.7% elongation, 98.9% density—marginal on ductility and density (yang2022developinganovel pages 1-5).
3. **Standard AlSi10Mg:** As-built YS ~240–270 MPa—**does not reach 300 MPa** (mehta2023developmentofhigh pages 66-69).
4. **Al–Mn–Cr (Zr-free ternary from the Mehta family):** Projected as-built YS ~200–250 MPa; aged YS may reach ~300 MPa—not directly demonstrated without Zr (mehta2022al–mn–cr–zrbasedalloystailored pages 2-3, mehta2022al–mn–cr–zrbasedalloystailored pages 3-4).
5. **Al–Mg–Si–Ti (Wen et al. 2024 concept, 0.77% Ti):** UTS 447.8 MPa, elongation 9.1% as-built—promising but Ti is the nucleant former, and the exact composition was not retrieved in full detail.
6. **AlSi11CuMn:** YS ~350 MPa as-built reported in a review (hussain2026metallurgicalaspectsof pages 5-7).

**Ranking by evidence strength:** The Al–Mg–Zn–Si–Mn composition has the strongest single-paper evidence for a Zr-free alloy exceeding 300 MPa, though its elongation and density are borderline. The pseudo-binary Al–Mg₂Si eutectic has the highest YS but fails ductility. Ti-containing Al–Mg–Si–Ti is the most mechanistically promising Zr-free route toward >400 MPa with ≥8% elongation, but requires validation of the specific composition. No Zr-free, Sc-free alloy in the retrieved evidence simultaneously meets YS >300 MPa, elongation ≥8%, and density ≥99.5%.

---

## 3. Microstructure Expectations for the Campaign's Route

The campaign uses ultrasonically atomized powder (D50 ~55–65 µm, cut to 20–63 µm), an Aconity MIDI (400 W-class, ~80 µm spot), and 30–50 µm layers. Key differences from the literature conditions:

**Coarser powder** (D50 ~40 vs. 15–37 µm in references): Coarser powder produces larger inter-particle voids and lower packing density, requiring higher VED to achieve full densification. Literature alloys like Addalloy used D50 14–37 µm (griffiths2020coarseningandcreep pages 2-3, griffiths2018effectoflaser pages 1-2), and CP1 used 60 µm layers with standard fine powder (pauzon2022anovellaser pages 1-4). Coarser feedstock may also have different chemistry (less surface oxide per unit mass but possibly different solidification history inside the particles).

**80 µm spot vs. 40–100 µm in references:** The 80 µm spot is similar to the EOS M290 (100 µm) used for most Mehta alloys and Bayoumy's alloy. The cooling rate will be on the order of 10⁵–10⁶ K/s, adequate for Mn/Cr/Mg supersaturation and primary Al₃Zr/Al₃Ti nucleation.

**Critical microstructural features by family:**
- **Al–Mn–Cr:** Success depends on Mn/Cr remaining in supersaturated solid solution (>3 wt% Mn metastably dissolved) (mair2022microstructuralfeaturesand pages 4-6). The coarser powder should not critically affect this, as supersaturation is determined by melt-pool cooling rate, not powder size.
- **Al–Mg–Si eutectic:** The α-Al/Mg₂Si eutectic spacing controls strength. Coarser powder and potentially lower cooling rate could coarsen the eutectic, reducing YS.
- **Al–Fe–Ni eutectic:** Similar eutectic-spacing sensitivity. The 80 µm spot should provide adequate refinement.
- **Mg loss:** At 810–840 °C atomization and during LPBF, Mg evaporation is significant for alloys with ≥5 wt% Mg. Add 0.5–1.0% excess Mg to the charge and verify by ICP-OES of both powder and printed material.

**25 °C vs. 150–200 °C plate preheat:** An unheated plate increases residual stress and cracking risk but preserves the supersaturated state. For Sc-containing alloys, a 200 °C plate can provide in-situ ageing equivalent to a post-build treatment (bayoumy2023effectiveplatformheating pages 1-2). For Al–Mn–Cr alloys, the ageing window is 350–400 °C, so a 150–200 °C plate should not cause premature precipitation. Using 150–200 °C for initial builds is recommended.

---

## 4. Direct Ageing Schedules and Expected Hardening

| Family | Direct-ageing schedule | Expected Δ | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Al–Mn–Cr–Zr | 375 °C/8–24 h | +40–50 HV; YS +100–110 MPa | No overageing seen through 2544 h at 250 °C; ~12% loss at 350 °C/1054 h (mehta2023advancingnovelalmncrzr pages 9-12, mehta2023developmentofhigh pages 66-69) |
| Al–Mg–Zr (Addalloy) | 400 °C/2–8 h | YS +100–130 MPa | Coarsening-resistant Al₃Zr; 60 h at 400 °C causes ~15% loss (griffiths2020coarseningandcreep pages 2-3, griffiths2020additivemanufacturingof pages 109-114) |
| Al–Fe–Zr (CP1) | 400 °C/4 h | YS → 310 MPa from ~200 as-built | Precipitation of Al₃Zr + Al₁₃Fe₄ raises conductivity simultaneously (pauzon2022anovellaser pages 1-4, pauzon2022anovellaser pages 8-12) |
| Al–Mg–Mn–Er–Zr | 375 °C/10 h (or 350 °C/25 h, 325 °C/50–100 h) | YS +115 MPa; HV +40 | Al₃(Er,Zr) core–shell precipitation; stable to ~400 °C (guo2022microstructureandmechanical pages 4-8) |
| Scalmalloy-type | 300–350 °C/4–12 h | YS → 460–520 MPa | 200 °C platform heating can partially substitute (hussain2026metallurgicalaspectsof pages 36-38, he2021designanddevelopment pages 40-45, bayoumy2023effectiveplatformheating pages 1-2) |
| AlSi10Mg | 160–170 °C/6 h | Modest YS increase | Coarsening of Si network above ~200 °C **reduces** strength; heated plate at 150–200 °C causes progressive softening (mehta2023developmentofhigh pages 66-69) |

**Families that lose strength on a heated plate or during stress relief:** AlSi10Mg is most sensitive—holding at 200+ °C coarsens the Si network and reduces as-built UTS. The Al–Mn–Cr system is robust through ~250 °C but loses hardness above 350 °C over long holds.

### Design Rationale

**Mechanistic diversity.** The six seeds cover: (1) eutectic Si network hardening (AlSi10Mg); (2) Mn/Cr supersaturated solid solution (Zr-free Al–Mn–Cr); (3) eutectic Mg₂Si + Al₃Ti nucleation (Al–Mg–Si–Ti); (4) Mg + Mn + Cr solution strengthening with deliberate cracking-boundary probing (Al–Mn–Cr–Mg); (5) eutectic Al–Fe–Ni intermetallic network (Al–Fe–Ni); (6) Er-based L1₂ precipitation without Zr (Al–Mg–Mn–Er). Each probes a different strengthening mechanism and different elements, maximising SAASBO information content across 15 candidate elements.

**Feedstock compatibility.** Seeds 1–4 and 6 use only elements on hand (Al from 6063/Al-12Si bar, Mg, Mn, Cr, Ti, Si, Er). Seed 5 requires purchasing Fe and Ni (described as quick to buy). The three optional seeds (7–9) all require purchasing Al–10Zr master alloy.

**Meltability.** All six primary seeds have estimated liquidus temperatures below ~700 °C, well within the 1300 °C induction-furnace capacity. The practical concern is not furnace temperature but rather primary intermetallic formation:
- **Al–Mn–Cr:** At ≥5 wt% Mn, the Mn-rich sludge region (Al₆Mn) may form if the melt is held below ~700 °C for extended periods. Rapid melting and immediate pouring into the atomizer is recommended.
- **Ti-containing alloys (Seed 3):** Al₃Ti has a peritectic temperature of ~665 °C. Ti should ideally be added as an Al–5Ti–1B rod or similar master alloy and dissolved at ≥750 °C, though the charge is small enough that dissolution should be rapid.
- **Er-containing alloys (Seed 6):** Al₃Er forms at ~640 °C. With only 0.3 wt% Er and a 350 g charge, dissolution at 810–840 °C should be achievable.

### What Is Known vs. Unknown for Each Seed

**Seed 1 (AlSi10Mg):** Well-established LPBF alloy with hundreds of publications. Expected to print without issue. Known: as-built YS ~230–270 MPa (mehta2023developmentofhigh pages 66-69). Unknown: exact performance with ultrasonically atomized coarser powder.

**Seed 2 (Zr-free Al–5Mn–0.8Cr):** The ternary without Zr has not been independently published as a tensile specimen—Mehta's Alloy A (Al–4.7Mn, no Cr, no Zr) and Alloy B (Al–0.8Mn–0.14Cr, no Zr) were ternaries tested only for hardness (~80–90 HV) (mehta2022al–mn–cr–zrbasedalloystailored pages 2-3). Crack-freedom is expected based on the Scheil design principle, but the ageing response without Zr precipitation hardening is uncertain.

**Seed 3 (Al–5Mg–2Si–0.7Ti):** Inspired by Wen et al.'s Al–Mg–Si–Ti (UTS 447.8 MPa, 9.1% elongation as-built) and Yang et al.'s high-Mg–Si alloys (yang2022developinganovel pages 1-5, yang2023microstructureandmechanical pages 1-2). The specific composition is *not a direct reproduction* of any single published alloy. Mg₂Si eutectic backfilling + Al₃Ti nucleation is the mechanism being tested.

**Seed 4 (Al–4.7Mn–0.8Cr–1.0Mg):** The closest literature alloy (Mehta Alloy E, with 0.7 wt% Zr) **cracked** (mehta2023advancingnovelalmncrzr pages 1-3, mehta2023advancingnovelalmncrzr pages 3-5). This seed deliberately probes whether the alloy cracks without Zr, providing essential boundary information for the optimizer.

**Seed 5 (Al–1.5Fe–1.5Ni):** An exploratory eutectic composition. Al–Fe–Ni eutectic alloys have been investigated for thermal stability but tensile data at this composition are sparse in the retrieved evidence. The narrow freezing range should favour printability.

**Seed 6 (Al–5Mg–0.7Mn–0.3Er):** No Zr-free Er alloy was found to be published as crack-free. This is a high-information exploratory seed to determine whether Al₃Er alone provides sufficient nucleation.

**Optional Seed 7 (Mehta Alloy F reproduction):** Directly reproduces the strongest documented result in the Al–Mn–Cr–Zr family: 500/560 MPa YS/UTS (mehta2023developmentofhigh pages 66-69). Requires Al–10Zr master alloy purchase.

**Optional Seed 8 (Guo Al–6Mg–0.7Mn–0.4Er–1.1Zr):** Reproduces the best Er-bearing result: 440/520 MPa YS/UTS with 15.5% elongation after 375 °C/10 h (guo2022microstructureandmechanical pages 4-8, guo2022microstructureandmechanical pages 3-4). Requires Zr and uses limited Er stock.

**Optional Seed 9 (Low-Sc Al–4Mg–0.3Sc–0.4Zr):** Tests whether 0.3% Sc with 0.4% Zr provides a useful fraction of Scalmalloy performance (~460–520 MPa) (hussain2026metallurgicalaspectsof pages 36-38, he2021designanddevelopment pages 40-45). Requires both Zr and uses limited Sc stock.

### Family (a): Al–Mn–Cr–Zr and Al–Mn–Ti–Zr

**Al–Mn–Cr–Zr (Mehta / Chalmers).** Mehta et al. developed a family of Al–Mn–Cr–Zr alloys specifically for LPBF, with compositions determined by ICP-OES at Höganäs AB (pqac-00000024). Alloy C (Al–5.0Mn–0.8Cr–0.6Zr–0.17Fe–0.24Si, measured) was processed on an EOS M100 (170 W, 1500 mm/s, 0.1 mm hatch, 30 µm layers) and later an EOS M290 (370 W, 1300 mm/s, 0.13 mm hatch, 30 µm layers, 100 µm spot), achieving 99.5–99.8% relative density and inherent crack-freedom across a broad DOE window (pqac-00000026, pqac-00000027). As-built tensile properties averaged across XZ/XY orientations were YS 250 MPa, UTS 310 MPa, and 25% elongation; after direct ageing at 648 K for 24 h these rose to YS 350 MPa, UTS 440 MPa, and 8% elongation, with hardness increasing from ~102 to ~130 HV (pqac-00000047).

Alloy F (Al–4.8Mn–0.9Cr–1.1Zr–1.2Mg, measured ICP-OES) introduced both increased Zr (beyond solubility, triggering grain refinement via primary L1₂-Al₃Zr) and Mg for solid-solution strengthening (pqac-00000024, pqac-00000025). It achieved 99.7–99.8% density and was crack-free, in contrast to Alloy E (Al–4.7Mn–0.8Cr–0.7Zr–1.0Mg) which cracked because its lower Zr content was insufficient for heterogeneous nucleation (pqac-00000025). Alloy F as-built: YS 390 MPa, UTS 450 MPa, 17% elongation; after ageing at 648 K for 8 h: YS 500 MPa, UTS 560 MPa, 5% elongation, hardness 132→172 HV (pqac-00000040, pqac-00000047). The Al-HS1 industrial variant of this family was qualified at component level by Arena et al. (2024); after 375 °C/14 h ageing, horizontal specimens achieved YS 356 MPa, UTS 441 MPa, and 10.4% elongation (pqac-00000045).

**Al–Mn–Ti–Zr (Mair et al.).** A novel Al–4.8Mn alloy modified with Ti and Zr was processed at 380 W, 1900 mm/s, 0.1 mm hatch, 30 µm layers on an unheated substrate (pqac-00000002). The as-built alloy achieved 99.9 ± 0.1% density, was crack-free, and had YS 284 ± 3 MPa, UTS 320 ± 1 MPa, and 16.9 ± 0.2% elongation with 108 ± 1 HV10, primarily from Mn supersaturation (3.7 ± 0.5 wt% retained in matrix) and fine-grain strengthening via primary L1₂-Al₃(Ti,Zr) nucleants (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000004).

### Family (b): Al–Mg–Zr (Addalloy)

Griffiths, Croteau, Dunand and coworkers studied Addalloy™ with measured ICP-OES compositions of Al–3.60Mg–1.18Zr (Batch 1) and Al–3.60Mg–1.12Zr (Batch 2) (pqac-00000048, pqac-00000049). Processing was on a Concept Laser M2 (200 W CW, 1070 nm, 90 µm spot) at 200 mm/s, 0.135 mm hatch, and 30–40 µm layers. As-fabricated YS ranged from ~220 MPa (Batch 1, lower Zr) to ~290 MPa (Batch 2, higher Zr) depending on batch and orientation. After peak ageing at 400 °C for 2–8 h, YS reached 345–359 MPa with ~20% elongation (pqac-00000055, pqac-00000048). The strengthening was dominated by coherent 2–5 nm L1₂-Al₃Zr precipitates formed during ageing, with Mg contributing solid-solution hardening.

### Family (c): Al–Fe–Zr (Aheadd CP1)

Pauzon et al. (2022) reported the Constellium Aheadd CP1 alloy with ICP-measured powder composition of Al–1.02Fe–1.05Zr (O 0.098, N <0.005, H 0.0019 wt%) (pqac-00000006). LPBF was performed on an EOS M290 at 370 W, 1400 mm/s, 0.13 mm hatch, 60 µm layers, with 100 °C platform preheating. Relative density exceeded 99.7%. After stress relief at 300 °C/2 h and direct ageing at 400 °C/4 h, the alloy reached YS 310 MPa with thermal conductivity of 180 W/m·K (pqac-00000006, pqac-00000007). The alloy exploits primary Al₃Zr for crack prevention and nanoscale Al₃Zr + Al₁₃Fe₄ precipitation for strengthening.

### Family (d): Al–Mg–Si Eutectic-Type Alloys (without Zr/Sc/Ti grain refiners)

Yang et al. (2023) processed a pseudo-binary Al–9.6Mg–4.9Si alloy (nominally Al–13.3 wt% Mg₂Si) by LPBF at VED 129.6 J/mm³, achieving 99.3% density and as-built YS 439 MPa, UTS 557 MPa, but only 2.9% elongation—far below the 8% target (pqac-00000013). A related Al–5.39Mg–3.08Zn–1.96Si–0.75Mn alloy (measured ICP) processed on a Farsoon FS271M at VED 129.1 J/mm³ achieved 403 MPa YS, 548 MPa UTS, and 6.7% elongation (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000014). These Zr-free, Si-free alloys demonstrate that high-Mg + Si eutectic compositions can reach >400 MPa YS as-built, but ductility and density are on the edge of the campaign requirements.

### Family (e): Modified Al–Si–Mg

The Al–Mg–Si–Zr alloy Al–7Mg–2Si–1.2Zr (nominal) by Yang et al. (2022) was processed at 170 W, 350 mm/s, 0.15 mm hatch, 30 µm layers, 150 °C plate, achieving as-built YS 447.9 ± 3.6 MPa, UTS 493.4 ± 6.7 MPa, and 9.6 ± 1.1% elongation (pqac-00000021, pqac-00000022). After HT2 (high-temperature ageing), YS further increased to 467 ± 1.3 MPa. This alloy requires Zr for grain refinement.

### Family (f): Er as Sc Substitute

Guo et al. (2022) demonstrated Al–Mg–Mn–Er–Zr alloys. The best performer, specimen 3# with measured composition Al–6.40Mg–0.72Mn–0.40Er–1.10Zr (pqac-00000054), was processed at 350 W, 1000 mm/s, 0.13 mm hatch, 30 µm layers (pqac-00000008). As-built: YS 325 ± 4 MPa, UTS 438 ± 3 MPa, 18.0 ± 1.8% elongation. After direct ageing at 375 °C/10 h: YS 440 ± 3 MPa, UTS 520 ± 2 MPa, 15.5 ± 1.0% elongation (pqac-00000051, pqac-00000052). The strengthening mechanism involves Al₃Er primary nucleation followed by Al₃(Er,Zr) core–shell precipitation. **No crack-free Er-bearing alloy without Zr was identified** in the retrieved literature.

**Al–Ni–Er–Zr (Taheri-Mousavi et al.).** The design composition was Al–2.73Ni–3.19Zr–2.33Er (wt%), ultrasonically atomized and LPBF-processed into crack-free specimens (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000016). The alloy exploits sub-micron metastable Al₂₃Ni₆M₄ ternary phases formed during rapid solidification as reservoirs for 1–5 nm coherent L1₂-Al₃(Er,Zr) nanoprecipitates upon ageing at 400 °C/8 h. As-built hardness was 180 HV; after ageing, peak tensile strength reached ~395 MPa, described as ~50% above the benchmark printable Al alloy and comparable to wrought Al 7075 (pqac-00000016). The design is thermally stable through 48 h at 400 °C.

### Family (g): Low-Sc Al–Mg–Sc–Zr and Al–Mn–Sc

Bayoumy et al. (2023) studied an Al–Mn–Sc alloy with measured composition Al–4.58Mn–1.24Mg–0.91Sc–0.42Zr (wt%, converted from at%) (pqac-00000017). Processed on an EOS M290 at 350 W, 1600 mm/s, 0.1 mm hatch, 30 µm layers, with 200 °C platform heating, the alloy achieved >99.5% density. The heated platform triggered in-situ ageing, precipitating 1.5–2 nm Sc-rich nanoclusters at 1.75 × 10²⁴ m⁻³ density, yielding YS 522 MPa with up to 18% elongation—without any post-build heat treatment (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000019). A related Al–3.04Mn–1.60Mg–0.78Sc–0.22Zr alloy (Zhang et al. 2023, measured) processed at large 120 µm layer thickness and heat-treated at 300 °C/5 h achieved YS 472 MPa and ~10% fracture strain (pqac-00000056, pqac-00000057). These results establish that ~0.8 wt% Sc with 0.2–0.4 wt% Zr is sufficient for fully equiaxed grains and excellent properties; reducing Sc below ~0.3 wt% risks incomplete refinement.

## 2. Zr-Free Compositions from Available Feedstock Exceeding ~300 MPa YS

The question restricts elements to Al, Si, Mg, Mn, Cr, Zn, Sn, Ti, Fe, Cu, Ni, Sc, and Er (no Zr, Ce, Li, Ag). Among compositions with published LPBF data:

1. **Al–9.6Mg–4.9Si (pseudo-binary Al–Mg₂Si eutectic):** YS 439 MPa, UTS 557 MPa, 2.9% elongation—**fails the ≥8% ductility criterion** (pqac-00000013).
2. **Al–5.39Mg–3.08Zn–1.96Si–0.75Mn (measured):** YS 403 MPa, UTS 548 MPa, 6.7% elongation, 98.9% density—marginal on ductility and density (pqac-00000012).
3. **Standard AlSi10Mg:** As-built YS ~240–270 MPa—**does not reach 300 MPa** (pqac-00000047).
4. **Al–Mn–Cr (Zr-free ternary from the Mehta family):** Projected as-built YS ~200–250 MPa; aged YS may reach ~300 MPa—not directly demonstrated without Zr (pqac-00000023, pqac-00000026).
5. **Al–Mg–Si–Ti (Wen et al. 2024 concept, 0.77% Ti):** UTS 447.8 MPa, elongation 9.1% as-built—promising but Ti is the nucleant former, and the exact composition was not retrieved in full detail.
6. **AlSi11CuMn:** YS ~350 MPa as-built reported in a review (pqac-00000032).

**Ranking by evidence strength:** The Al–Mg–Zn–Si–Mn composition has the strongest single-paper evidence for a Zr-free alloy exceeding 300 MPa, though its elongation and density are borderline. The pseudo-binary Al–Mg₂Si eutectic has the highest YS but fails ductility. Ti-containing Al–Mg–Si–Ti is the most mechanistically promising Zr-free route toward >400 MPa with ≥8% elongation, but requires validation of the specific composition. No Zr-free, Sc-free alloy in the retrieved evidence simultaneously meets YS >300 MPa, elongation ≥8%, and density ≥99.5%.

## 3. Microstructure Expectations for the Campaign's Route

The campaign uses ultrasonically atomized powder (D50 ~55–65 µm, cut to 20–63 µm), an Aconity MIDI (400 W-class, ~80 µm spot), and 30–50 µm layers. Key differences from the literature conditions:

**Coarser powder** (D50 ~40 vs. 15–37 µm in references): Coarser powder produces larger inter-particle voids and lower packing density, requiring higher VED to achieve full densification. Literature alloys like Addalloy used D50 14–37 µm (pqac-00000048, pqac-00000049), and CP1 used 60 µm layers with standard fine powder (pqac-00000006). Coarser feedstock may also have different chemistry (less surface oxide per unit mass but possibly different solidification history inside the particles).

**80 µm spot vs. 40–100 µm in references:** The 80 µm spot is similar to the EOS M290 (100 µm) used for most Mehta alloys and Bayoumy's alloy. The cooling rate will be on the order of 10⁵–10⁶ K/s, adequate for Mn/Cr/Mg supersaturation and primary Al₃Zr/Al₃Ti nucleation.

**Critical microstructural features by family:**
- **Al–Mn–Cr:** Success depends on Mn/Cr remaining in supersaturated solid solution (>3 wt% Mn metastably dissolved) (pqac-00000003). The coarser powder should not critically affect this, as supersaturation is determined by melt-pool cooling rate, not powder size.
- **Al–Mg–Si eutectic:** The α-Al/Mg₂Si eutectic spacing controls strength. Coarser powder and potentially lower cooling rate could coarsen the eutectic, reducing YS.
- **Al–Fe–Ni eutectic:** Similar eutectic-spacing sensitivity. The 80 µm spot should provide adequate refinement.
- **Mg loss:** At 810–840 °C atomization and during LPBF, Mg evaporation is significant for alloys with ≥5 wt% Mg. Add 0.5–1.0% excess Mg to the charge and verify by ICP-OES of both powder and printed material.

**25 °C vs. 150–200 °C plate preheat:** An unheated plate increases residual stress and cracking risk but preserves the supersaturated state. For Sc-containing alloys, a 200 °C plate can provide in-situ ageing equivalent to a post-build treatment (pqac-00000018). For Al–Mn–Cr alloys, the ageing window is 350–400 °C, so a 150–200 °C plate should not cause premature precipitation. Using 150–200 °C for initial builds is recommended.

*Table: Recommended six initial alloys and three optional additions, with feedstock, processing rationale, evidence targets, risks, and ageing schedules. Estimates and unsupported extrapolations are explicitly separated from published results.*

### Design Rationale

**Mechanistic diversity.** The six seeds cover: (1) eutectic Si network hardening (AlSi10Mg); (2) Mn/Cr supersaturated solid solution (Zr-free Al–Mn–Cr); (3) eutectic Mg₂Si + Al₃Ti nucleation (Al–Mg–Si–Ti); (4) Mg + Mn + Cr solution strengthening with deliberate cracking-boundary probing (Al–Mn–Cr–Mg); (5) eutectic Al–Fe–Ni intermetallic network (Al–Fe–Ni); (6) Er-based L1₂ precipitation without Zr (Al–Mg–Mn–Er). Each probes a different strengthening mechanism and different elements, maximising SAASBO information content across 15 candidate elements.

**Feedstock compatibility.** Seeds 1–4 and 6 use only elements on hand (Al from 6063/Al-12Si bar, Mg, Mn, Cr, Ti, Si, Er). Seed 5 requires purchasing Fe and Ni (described as quick to buy). The three optional seeds (7–9) all require purchasing Al–10Zr master alloy.

**Meltability.** All six primary seeds have estimated liquidus temperatures below ~700 °C, well within the 1300 °C induction-furnace capacity. The practical concern is not furnace temperature but rather primary intermetallic formation:
- **Al–Mn–Cr:** At ≥5 wt% Mn, the Mn-rich sludge region (Al₆Mn) may form if the melt is held below ~700 °C for extended periods. Rapid melting and immediate pouring into the atomizer is recommended.
- **Ti-containing alloys (Seed 3):** Al₃Ti has a peritectic temperature of ~665 °C. Ti should ideally be added as an Al–5Ti–1B rod or similar master alloy and dissolved at ≥750 °C, though the charge is small enough that dissolution should be rapid.
- **Er-containing alloys (Seed 6):** Al₃Er forms at ~640 °C. With only 0.3 wt% Er and a 350 g charge, dissolution at 810–840 °C should be achievable.

### What Is Known vs. Unknown for Each Seed

**Seed 1 (AlSi10Mg):** Well-established LPBF alloy with hundreds of publications. Expected to print without issue. Known: as-built YS ~230–270 MPa (pqac-00000047). Unknown: exact performance with ultrasonically atomized coarser powder.

**Seed 2 (Zr-free Al–5Mn–0.8Cr):** The ternary without Zr has not been independently published as a tensile specimen—Mehta's Alloy A (Al–4.7Mn, no Cr, no Zr) and Alloy B (Al–0.8Mn–0.14Cr, no Zr) were ternaries tested only for hardness (~80–90 HV) (pqac-00000023). Crack-freedom is expected based on the Scheil design principle, but the ageing response without Zr precipitation hardening is uncertain.

**Seed 3 (Al–5Mg–2Si–0.7Ti):** Inspired by Wen et al.'s Al–Mg–Si–Ti (UTS 447.8 MPa, 9.1% elongation as-built) and Yang et al.'s high-Mg–Si alloys (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000013). The specific composition is *not a direct reproduction* of any single published alloy. Mg₂Si eutectic backfilling + Al₃Ti nucleation is the mechanism being tested.

**Seed 4 (Al–4.7Mn–0.8Cr–1.0Mg):** The closest literature alloy (Mehta Alloy E, with 0.7 wt% Zr) **cracked** (pqac-00000024, pqac-00000025). This seed deliberately probes whether the alloy cracks without Zr, providing essential boundary information for the optimizer.

**Seed 5 (Al–1.5Fe–1.5Ni):** An exploratory eutectic composition. Al–Fe–Ni eutectic alloys have been investigated for thermal stability but tensile data at this composition are sparse in the retrieved evidence. The narrow freezing range should favour printability.

**Seed 6 (Al–5Mg–0.7Mn–0.3Er):** No Zr-free Er alloy was found to be published as crack-free. This is a high-information exploratory seed to determine whether Al₃Er alone provides sufficient nucleation.

**Optional Seed 7 (Mehta Alloy F reproduction):** Directly reproduces the strongest documented result in the Al–Mn–Cr–Zr family: 500/560 MPa YS/UTS (pqac-00000047). Requires Al–10Zr master alloy purchase.

**Optional Seed 8 (Guo Al–6Mg–0.7Mn–0.4Er–1.1Zr):** Reproduces the best Er-bearing result: 440/520 MPa YS/UTS with 15.5% elongation after 375 °C/10 h (pqac-00000051, pqac-00000052). Requires Zr and uses limited Er stock.

**Optional Seed 9 (Low-Sc Al–4Mg–0.3Sc–0.4Zr):** Tests whether 0.3% Sc with 0.4% Zr provides a useful fraction of Scalmalloy performance (~460–520 MPa) (pqac-00000038, pqac-00000039). Requires both Zr and uses limited Sc stock.

contexts.context: The excerpt reports ML-guided Al-alloy design. Spearman analysis found Zr most reduces coarsening, while Er most increases L1₂ atomic fraction; Er and Yb strongly affect solidification range, and Y/Ni influence ternary phases. Neural-network prediction reached ~3% normalized error with 40 compositions, versus ~20% for linear regression, indicating nonlinearity. Bayesian optimization predicted that high Zr requires Er to dissolve Zr into beneficial ternary L1₂ phases; otherwise brittle Al₃Zr forms. The optimized alloy achieved 40% higher L1₂ fraction and 3.5× lower coarsening metric while satisfying printability criteria. Al₃Ni improves printability but is soft and coarsens rapidly.
contexts.question:
We must pick the first SIX aluminium alloy compositions (plus three optional extras) for a laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) alloy discovery campaign, and write a complete recipe for each. Please do a deep, quantitative literature review that lets us choose and specify them. Report MEASURED chemistries (ICP/OES of powder or part) rather than nominal ones wherever the paper gives them, and say which is which.

CONTEXT
- Goal: an alloy that is stronger than LPBF AlSi10Mg (as-built yield about 230-300 MPa) without relying on critical minerals, and/or one that approaches Scalmalloy (Al-4.6Mg-0.7Sc-0.3Zr, about 470-520 MPa yield when direct aged) with much less Sc. Strength first; ductility of at least about 8 %; relative density at least 99.5 %; crack-free.
- Powder: made in-house by 40 kHz ultrasonic atomization of 170-350 g charges melted by induction at up to about 1300 C (so far run at 810-840 C), collected under argon. Median size is coarse (D50 roughly 55-65 um), so the LPBF cut will probably be 20-63 um.
- Feedstock on hand: 6063 bar (carries about 0.5 Mg, 0.4 Si, 0.2 Fe), Al-12Si (4047) bar, Mg, Mn, Cr, Zn, Sn, Ti, Si, and small amounts of Sc and Er. Quick to buy: Fe, Cu, Ni. NOT yet on hand and uncertain: Zr (would come as Al-10Zr master alloy), Ce, Li.
- Printer: Aconity MIDI (400 W-class single-mode fibre laser, about 80 um spot), argon, build-plate heating available. Sub-size tensile bars, as-built and direct-aged.
- After the six seeds a sparse-axis-aligned-subspace Bayesian optimizer (SAASBO) picks the remaining runs over about 15 candidate elements, so the seeds should be mechanistically diverse, not six variants of one family.

QUESTIONS
1. For each family below, give the best-documented specific composition(s) and, per paper: measured composition (wt%), powder route and size, LPBF machine, laser power, scan speed, hatch, layer thickness, spot size, plate preheat, volumetric energy density, relative density, cracking observations, as-built and heat-treated yield strength / UTS / elongation (with build orientation and heat treatment), hardness, and the microstructure reported (grain size and morphology, primary and eutectic phases, precipitates, retained solute). Families:
   a. Al-Mn-Cr-Zr (Chalmers group: Mehta, Nyborg, Hryha and co-workers) and Al-Mn-Ti-Zr (Mair et al.), and Zr-free Al-Mn-Cr or Al-Mn-Mg variants.
   b. Al-Mg-Zr (Croteau, Dunand, Seidman et al.; Addalloy) and Al-Mg-Zr-Mn.
   c. Al-Fe-Zr (Constellium Aheadd CP1 type), Al-Fe-Mg-Zr (Li et al. 2025), binary Al-Fe (Qi, Takata, Kimura), Al-Fe-Cr, Al-Fe-Mn, Al-Fe-Cu, Al-Fe-Ni (AlFeNi eutectic) and Al-Fe-V-Si (8009).
   d. Al-Mg-Si eutectic-type alloys with high Mg (Al-Mg2Si pseudo-binary, Magsimal-59-like AlMg5Si2Mn, Fehrmann AlMgty, the Dreano Al-6.7Mg-3Si-1.4Ni-1Zn alloy) that print crack-free WITHOUT Zr, Sc or Ti grain refiners.
   e. Modified Al-Si-Mg: AlSi7Mg0.6 (A357), AlSi10Mg with raised Mg (1-3 wt%), with Mn, Cu, Ni, Er, Zr or Sc additions; Al-Si-Ni and Al-Si-Fe-Mn; which of these beat standard AlSi10Mg as-built or direct-aged, and by how much.
   f. Er as a Sc substitute: Al-Mg-Er-Zr, Al-Mg-Mn-Er-Zr, Al-Er-Zr, Al-Zr-Er-Yb, Al-Ni-Er-Zr (Taheri-Mousavi et al.). Is there any crack-free Er-bearing alloy WITHOUT Zr?
   g. Low-Sc Al-Mg-Sc-Zr (Sc 0.1-0.4 wt%) and low-Sc Al-Mn-Sc; the lowest Sc level that still gives equiaxed, crack-free builds and an ageing response; Sc partially replaced by Zr, Er, Ti or Y.
   h. Al-Ce(-Mg, -Mn, -Ni, -Zr), Al-Ni(-Mn, -Zr, -Sc), Al-Cu-Mn-Zr (ACMZ), Al-Cu-Mg with Ti, Zr or TiB2 (A20X, 2024+Zr), 7xxx with Zr (HRL 7A77) or with Si, and 6061 with Zr or Si.
   i. Ti as the L1_2 / D0_22 former instead of Zr: Al-Ti, Al-Mg-Ti, Al-Mn-Ti, Al-Cu-Ti, Ti-modified 2xxx/7xxx, Al-5Ti-1B (TiB2) inoculated alloys made by melt routes.
2. Zr is not yet on our shelf. Which compositions made ONLY from Al, Si, Mg, Mn, Cr, Zn, Sn, Ti, Fe, Cu, Ni, Sc and Er (no Zr, Ce, Li, Ag) have been printed crack-free by LPBF with as-built or aged yield strength above about 300 MPa? Rank them by evidence.
3. For each of the top candidates, what microstructure should we expect from OUR route (coarser 20-63 um ultrasonically atomized powder, 80 um spot, 30-50 um layers, with 25 C versus 150-200 C plate), and which features decide success (primary Al3Zr/Al3Ti nucleants at the melt-pool boundary, eutectic fraction, Mn/Cr supersaturation, Mg loss)?
4. Direct ageing (no solution treatment) schedules and expected hardening for each family, and which families lose strength on a heated plate or in stress relief.
5. Recommend a set of six seeds (2 benchmarks, 3 literature picks, 1 exploratory) and three optional extras that are (i) mechanistically diverse, (ii) makeable from the feedstock above (flag each element that must be bought), (iii) meltable and castable below about 1000 C without primary Al3Zr / Al3Ti / Al-Cr-Mn sludge in the crucible (give the liquidus where known), and (iv) each informative about a different strengthening route. State what is known and unknown for each, and which published result we would be trying to reproduce.

Give DOIs for every source and separate what the papers state from your inference.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes an Al–Ni–Zr–Er–Y–Yb design, but gives no measured/nominal composition, powder chemistry, LPBF parameters, density, or tensile values. Rapid solidification produced nanoscale ternary L1₂ phases and avoided coarse Zr-rich phases; induction-cast material formed microscale ternary/L1₂ phases and had five-times lower hardness. Removing Ni caused grain-interior Zr-rich phases and 34% lower hardness. Printed material achieved 50% higher hardness and peak tensile strength than a benchmark after 8 h at 400 °C, comparable hardness to wrought Al7075, and no strength drop after 48 h at 400 °C. L1₂ strengthening follows Orowan behavior, approximately inversely with precipitate radius; ~17 nm particles are identified as optimal for creep.

contexts.context: The excerpt concerns Bayoumy et al.’s Al-Mn-Sc-Zr alloy fabricated by laser powder bed fusion (LPBF), comparing as-fabricated material (AF) with material produced using a 200 °C heated platform (AF-200). It states that platform heating reduces residual stresses to approximately 57% of those in the unheated AF material and improves tensile properties. AF-200 achieves an attractive strength–ductility combination in the as-built condition, without post-processing artificial aging; its yield strength is described as exceeding that of most LPBF Al-Sc alloys, including Scalmalloy, and as comparable to a similar alloy in the peak-aged condition. The APT results identify numerous fine, nearly spherical Sc-rich precipitates in AF-200, with a measured cluster composition of approximately 72 at.% Al, 20 at.% Sc, 3.6 at.% Mg, 3.2 at.% Mn, and 1.4 at.% Zr. The nominal Sc content reported for the alloy is 0.56 at.%, while approximately 0.41 at.% Sc remains in solid solution after in situ heating. The excerpt does not provide the alloy’s complete nominal composition, detailed LPBF process parameters, numerical as-built or aged mechanical-property values, or the exact AF-200 yield strength; those values would need to be obtained from other sections or tables of the article.

contexts.context: Bayoumy et al. investigated an Al-Mn-Sc-Zr alloy whose measured composition was Al-2.32Mn-1.42Mg-0.56Sc-0.13Zr-0.03Fe-0.04Si in atomic percent, equivalent to Al-4.58Mn-1.24Mg-0.91Sc-0.42Zr-0.07Fe-0.04Si in weight percent. The scandium content was therefore 0.56 at.% or 0.91 wt.%. The gas-atomized powder had particles ranging from 20–70 µm, averaging approximately 35 µm. LPBF was performed on an EOS M290 using a 350 W Yb-fiber laser, 1600 mm/s scan speed, 0.1 mm hatch spacing, 30 µm layer thickness, and 67° alternating scan rotation under argon with oxygen below 0.1 vol.%. Builds used either a 35°C platform (AF) or a 200°C platform (AF-200), and both achieved over 99.5% densification. The excerpt explains that 200°C platform heating improved strength by approximately 50–100 MPa relative to the 35°C condition and was intended to provide in situ aging and reduce residual stress. contexts.context: The excerpt identifies the material as a high-strength Al-Mn-Sc-based alloy processed by laser powder bed fusion, but it does not provide the alloy’s full chemical composition, the numerical Sc content, or the detailed LPBF process parameters. It also does not report a complete comparison of as-built and conventionally aged mechanical properties. The available results show that heating the platform to 200 °C largely relieved process-induced residual stresses relative to an unheated 35 °C platform. The heating promoted in situ aging and dynamic precipitation of uniformly dispersed Sc-rich nanoclusters measuring approximately 1.5–2 nm, with a reported number density of 1.75 × 10^24 m−3. This produced approximately a 20% increase in tensile yield strength, reaching 522 MPa, while retaining ductility of up to 18%. The excerpt therefore supports a platform-heated yield strength of 522 MPa, but the requested alloy composition, exact Sc concentration, LPBF parameters, and full as-built/aged property data would need to be obtained from later sections or tables of the article.

contexts.context: The alloy composition was Al–7Mg–2Si–1.2Zr, in weight percent. The LPBF system used a 170 W laser, 100 µm beam diameter, 30 µm layer thickness, 150 µm hatch spacing, argon shielding with oxygen below 0.15%, a 5 mm chessboard scan strategy, 67° layer-to-layer rotation, and a 150 °C build-plate temperature. The scan-speed optimization tested 300–475 mm/s and volumetric energy densities of 79.5–125.9 J·mm−3; the selected condition was 350 mm/s and 107.9 J·mm−3. The heat treatment associated with the high-strength condition was HT1 artificial aging at 180 °C for 4 h, intended to produce Mg2Si precipitation while limiting elongation loss. contexts.context: The excerpt examines Alloy C LPBF microstructure. Builds achieved about **99.6% average relative density**; optical sections covered **XY, YZ, and XZ** orientations. As-printed material showed **columnar grains along build direction**, finer grains in the XY plane, and similar morphology across alloys. Compared with atomized powder, printed material was emphasized because it represents application conditions. Solidification structure was predominantly dendritic, with **negligible precipitation at low magnification**; some interdendritic precipitates were **<100 nm**. BSE-SEM identified two nanometric precipitate populations: at **melt-pool boundaries** and at **grain/cell boundaries**.
contexts.question:
We must pick the first SIX aluminium alloy compositions (plus three optional extras) for a laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) alloy discovery campaign, and write a complete recipe for each. Please do a deep, quantitative literature review that lets us choose and specify them. Report MEASURED chemistries (ICP/OES of powder or part) rather than nominal ones wherever the paper gives them, and say which is which.

CONTEXT
- Goal: an alloy that is stronger than LPBF AlSi10Mg (as-built yield about 230-300 MPa) without relying on critical minerals, and/or one that approaches Scalmalloy (Al-4.6Mg-0.7Sc-0.3Zr, about 470-520 MPa yield when direct aged) with much less Sc. Strength first; ductility of at least about 8 %; relative density at least 99.5 %; crack-free.
- Powder: made in-house by 40 kHz ultrasonic atomization of 170-350 g charges melted by induction at up to about 1300 C (so far run at 810-840 C), collected under argon. Median size is coarse (D50 roughly 55-65 um), so the LPBF cut will probably be 20-63 um.
- Feedstock on hand: 6063 bar (carries about 0.5 Mg, 0.4 Si, 0.2 Fe), Al-12Si (4047) bar, Mg, Mn, Cr, Zn, Sn, Ti, Si, and small amounts of Sc and Er. Quick to buy: Fe, Cu, Ni. NOT yet on hand and uncertain: Zr (would come as Al-10Zr master alloy), Ce, Li.
- Printer: Aconity MIDI (400 W-class single-mode fibre laser, about 80 um spot), argon, build-plate heating available. Sub-size tensile bars, as-built and direct-aged.
- After the six seeds a sparse-axis-aligned-subspace Bayesian optimizer (SAASBO) picks the remaining runs over about 15 candidate elements, so the seeds should be mechanistically diverse, not six variants of one family.

QUESTIONS
1. For each family below, give the best-documented specific composition(s) and, per paper: measured composition (wt%), powder route and size, LPBF machine, laser power, scan speed, hatch, layer thickness, spot size, plate preheat, volumetric energy density, relative density, cracking observations, as-built and heat-treated yield strength / UTS / elongation (with build orientation and heat treatment), hardness, and the microstructure reported (grain size and morphology, primary and eutectic phases, precipitates, retained solute). Families:
   a. Al-Mn-Cr-Zr (Chalmers group: Mehta, Nyborg, Hryha and co-workers) and Al-Mn-Ti-Zr (Mair et al.), and Zr-free Al-Mn-Cr or Al-Mn-Mg variants.
   b. Al-Mg-Zr (Croteau, Dunand, Seidman et al.; Addalloy) and Al-Mg-Zr-Mn.
   c. Al-Fe-Zr (Constellium Aheadd CP1 type), Al-Fe-Mg-Zr (Li et al. 2025), binary Al-Fe (Qi, Takata, Kimura), Al-Fe-Cr, Al-Fe-Mn, Al-Fe-Cu, Al-Fe-Ni (AlFeNi eutectic) and Al-Fe-V-Si (8009).
   d. Al-Mg-Si eutectic-type alloys with high Mg (Al-Mg2Si pseudo-binary, Magsimal-59-like AlMg5Si2Mn, Fehrmann AlMgty, the Dreano Al-6.7Mg-3Si-1.4Ni-1Zn alloy) that print crack-free WITHOUT Zr, Sc or Ti grain refiners.
   e. Modified Al-Si-Mg: AlSi7Mg0.6 (A357), AlSi10Mg with raised Mg (1-3 wt%), with Mn, Cu, Ni, Er, Zr or Sc additions; Al-Si-Ni and Al-Si-Fe-Mn; which of these beat standard AlSi10Mg as-built or direct-aged, and by how much.
   f. Er as a Sc substitute: Al-Mg-Er-Zr, Al-Mg-Mn-Er-Zr, Al-Er-Zr, Al-Zr-Er-Yb, Al-Ni-Er-Zr (Taheri-Mousavi et al.). Is there any crack-free Er-bearing alloy WITHOUT Zr?
   g. Low-Sc Al-Mg-Sc-Zr (Sc 0.1-0.4 wt%) and low-Sc Al-Mn-Sc; the lowest Sc level that still gives equiaxed, crack-free builds and an ageing response; Sc partially replaced by Zr, Er, Ti or Y.
   h. Al-Ce(-Mg, -Mn, -Ni, -Zr), Al-Ni(-Mn, -Zr, -Sc), Al-Cu-Mn-Zr (ACMZ), Al-Cu-Mg with Ti, Zr or TiB2 (A20X, 2024+Zr), 7xxx with Zr (HRL 7A77) or with Si, and 6061 with Zr or Si.
   i. Ti as the L1_2 / D0_22 former instead of Zr: Al-Ti, Al-Mg-Ti, Al-Mn-Ti, Al-Cu-Ti, Ti-modified 2xxx/7xxx, Al-5Ti-1B (TiB2) inoculated alloys made by melt routes.
2. Zr is not yet on our shelf. Which compositions made ONLY from Al, Si, Mg, Mn, Cr, Zn, Sn, Ti, Fe, Cu, Ni, Sc and Er (no Zr, Ce, Li, Ag) have been printed crack-free by LPBF with as-built or aged yield strength above about 300 MPa? Rank them by evidence.
3. For each of the top candidates, what microstructure should we expect from OUR route (coarser 20-63 um ultrasonically atomized powder, 80 um spot, 30-50 um layers, with 25 C versus 150-200 C plate), and which features decide success (primary Al3Zr/Al3Ti nucleants at the melt-pool boundary, eutectic fraction, Mn/Cr supersaturation, Mg loss)?
4. Direct ageing (no solution treatment) schedules and expected hardening for each family, and which families lose strength on a heated plate or in stress relief.
5. Recommend a set of six seeds (2 benchmarks, 3 literature picks, 1 exploratory) and three optional extras that are (i) mechanistically diverse, (ii) makeable from the feedstock above (flag each element that must be bought), (iii) meltable and castable below about 1000 C without primary Al3Zr / Al3Ti / Al-Cr-Mn sludge in the crucible (give the liquidus where known), and (iv) each informative about a different strengthening route. State what is known and unknown for each, and which published result we would be trying to reproduce.

Give DOIs for every source and separate what the papers state from your inference.

contexts.context: The 2022 study designed crack-resistant Al alloys using solubility/misfit calculations and Scheil slopes. Atomization introduced unavoidable Fe and Si impurities (<0.2 wt%). Alloy C had a solidification slope near AlSi10Mg and negligible cracking susceptibility; 1 wt% each Fe/Si would significantly alter solidification, whereas 0.15 wt% each had negligible effect. On an EOS M100, optimum parameters were 170 W, 1500 mm/s, 0.1 mm hatch, 0.03 mm layers, producing 99.5–99.6% relative density with no observed cracks. Ageing near 623–723 K and nanometric Al₃Zr precipitates were discussed; precipitation could add 30–35 HV.

contexts.context: The Chalmers study used ICP-OES-measured, gas-atomized 20–53 µm powders: C Al–5.0Mn–0.8Cr–0.6Zr, D 4.7–0.8–1.2–0, E 4.7–0.8–0.7–1.0, F 4.8–0.9–1.1–1.2 (all wt%; Mg, Fe, Si traces listed). Increased Zr refined grains; Mg strengthened solid solution. Direct ageing was at 623/648 K.

contexts.context: The study’s Al–Mn–Cr–Zr framework targets “inherently crack-free” alloys via narrow solidification ranges and low end-of-solidification \(dT/d(f_s^{12})\). Zr-high variants formed primary cubic L1₂-Al₃Zr (1.42 versus 0.78 vol%), refining EBSD grain size from ~26 µm (alloy C) to ~1 µm (alloy F). EOS M290 densities reached 99.7–99.8%. Mg-free C/D had subsurface porosity; Zr-low Mg alloy E cracked, while Zr-high Mg alloy F did not. Mg segregated locally (~6× EDS counts); Mn-rich boundary precipitates remained. Precipitate ECD increased 0.10→0.15 µm and area fraction 0.016→0.084.

It defines precipitate/matrix lattice misfit as \(\varepsilon=100|1-a/a_m|\), and uses misfit multiplied by inverse diffusion resistivity as an \(L1_2\) coarsening metric. contexts.context: APT of LPBF samples found fine Zr-rich L1₂ precipitates and a large ternary Al–Ni–Er/Zr phase; precipitates were segmented at 3.0% Zr and the large phase at 2.5% Ni. APT used 40 K, 100 kHz, 15% pulse fraction, and 0.5% detection rate. High-throughput analysis varied Ni, Er, Zr, Y, and Yb (at.%): Zr most increased diffusion resistivity (Spearman +0.78) and reduced coarsening; Yb decreased resistivity (−0.35). Diffusion resistivity reduced coarsening with coefficient −0.96, versus misfit strain −0.22. Er most increased L1₂ fraction; Er/Yb improved heat-check resistance, while Yb suppressed ternary eutectics.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides limited evidence for the requested zirconium-, scandium-, and cerium-free LPBF aluminium systems. For the Al-Mg-Si category, commercial AA6061 is discussed, but the passage reports hot cracking and excessive porosity during initial LPBF fabrication rather than a yield strength above 300 MPa. Crack-free AA6061 was obtained by heating the powder bed to 500 °C, while another reported strategy used Zr or YSZ nucleants; however, no qualifying as-built or aged yield-strength value is given for unmodified AA6061. Scalmalloy® and the Al-Mn-Sc alloy achieve high strengths (520 MPa and 560 MPa, respectively), but they contain scandium and/or zirconium and therefore do not satisfy the stated exclusions. The Al-Zn-Mg(-Cu) discussion likewise emphasizes cracking, porosity, and inferior mechanical properties relative to wrought alloys; the successful AA7075 approach used Zr nano-nucleants. The excerpt does not report qualifying yield strengths above 300 MPa for Al-Si-Mg, Al-Mg-Si, Al-Mn-Cr, Al-Fe-Ni, or Al-Mg-Zn-Si alloys without Zr, Sc, or Ce.

contexts.context: The excerpt identifies several zirconium-, scandium-, and cerium-free LPBF aluminum compositions with yield strength above 300 MPa. For Al-Si-based materials, the cited Al-Si eutectic structure produced by LPBF achieved approximately 400 MPa yield strength and over 450 MPa ultimate tensile strength; the passage does not explicitly label this alloy as AlSi10Mg, so its exact Mg content should be verified. AlSi10Mg is also reported to benefit substantially from aging/post-processing: modified T5 treatment at 200 °C increased yield strength by 64% through nanoscale silicon precipitation, although the excerpt does not provide the resulting absolute yield strength. AlSi11CuMn, which contains no Zr, Sc, or Ce, reached 350 MPa yield strength in the LPBF-produced condition, exceeding the 300 MPa threshold; solution treatment and aging reduced its yield strength to 288 MPa while improving elongation. The excerpt does not report qualifying yield-strength values for the specifically requested Al-Mg-Si, Al-Mn-Cr, Al-Fe-Ni, or Al-Mg-Zn-Si compositions. Scalmalloy and Al-6.2Mg-0.36Sc-0.09Zr are excluded because they contain Sc and/or Zr.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides direct evidence for several LPBF aluminum compositions without reported zirconium, scandium, or cerium that exceed 300 MPa yield strength. Printed Al7075 (an Al–Zn–Mg–Cu alloy) achieved a yield strength of 325–373 MPa; the passage does not explicitly identify a Zr, Sc, or Ce addition for this result. A modified Al–Zn–Mg–Cu alloy containing TiC nanoparticles and TiH2 reached 485 MPa yield strength and 593 MPa ultimate tensile strength in crack-free parts. A Si-modified 7075 composition, described as an Al–Si–Zn–Mg–Cu hybrid, produced crack-free LPBF samples with 350 MPa yield strength and 415 MPa ultimate tensile strength after aging. These are the clearest qualifying results in the excerpt.
