contexts.question:
We must pick the first SIX aluminium alloy compositions (plus three optional extras) for a laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) alloy discovery campaign, and write a complete recipe for each. Please do a deep, quantitative literature review that lets us choose and specify them. Report MEASURED chemistries (ICP/OES of powder or part) rather than nominal ones wherever the paper gives them, and say which is which.

CONTEXT
- Goal: an alloy that is stronger than LPBF AlSi10Mg (as-built yield about 230-300 MPa) without relying on critical minerals, and/or one that approaches Scalmalloy (Al-4.6Mg-0.7Sc-0.3Zr, about 470-520 MPa yield when direct aged) with much less Sc. Strength first; ductility of at least about 8 %; relative density at least 99.5 %; crack-free.
- Powder: made in-house by 40 kHz ultrasonic atomization of 170-350 g charges melted by induction at up to about 1300 C (so far run at 810-840 C), collected under argon. Median size is coarse (D50 roughly 55-65 um), so the LPBF cut will probably be 20-63 um.
- Feedstock on hand: 6063 bar (carries about 0.5 Mg, 0.4 Si, 0.2 Fe), Al-12Si (4047) bar, Mg, Mn, Cr, Zn, Sn, Ti, Si, and small amounts of Sc and Er. Quick to buy: Fe, Cu, Ni. NOT yet on hand and uncertain: Zr (would come as Al-10Zr master alloy), Ce, Li.
- Printer: Aconity MIDI (400 W-class single-mode fibre laser, about 80 um spot), argon, build-plate heating available. Sub-size tensile bars, as-built and direct-aged.
- After the six seeds a sparse-axis-aligned-subspace Bayesian optimizer (SAASBO) picks the remaining runs over about 15 candidate elements, so the seeds should be mechanistically diverse, not six variants of one family.

QUESTIONS
1. For each family below, give the best-documented specific composition(s) and, per paper: measured composition (wt%), powder route and size, LPBF machine, laser power, scan speed, hatch, layer thickness, spot size, plate preheat, volumetric energy density, relative density, cracking observations, as-built and heat-treated yield strength / UTS / elongation (with build orientation and heat treatment), hardness, and the microstructure reported (grain size and morphology, primary and eutectic phases, precipitates, retained solute). Families:
   a. Al-Mn-Cr-Zr (Chalmers group: Mehta, Nyborg, Hryha and co-workers) and Al-Mn-Ti-Zr (Mair et al.), and Zr-free Al-Mn-Cr or Al-Mn-Mg variants.
   b. Al-Mg-Zr (Croteau, Dunand, Seidman et al.; Addalloy) and Al-Mg-Zr-Mn.
   c. Al-Fe-Zr (Constellium Aheadd CP1 type), Al-Fe-Mg-Zr (Li et al. 2025), binary Al-Fe (Qi, Takata, Kimura), Al-Fe-Cr, Al-Fe-Mn, Al-Fe-Cu, Al-Fe-Ni (AlFeNi eutectic) and Al-Fe-V-Si (8009).
   d. Al-Mg-Si eutectic-type alloys with high Mg (Al-Mg2Si pseudo-binary, Magsimal-59-like AlMg5Si2Mn, Fehrmann AlMgty, the Dreano Al-6.7Mg-3Si-1.4Ni-1Zn alloy) that print crack-free WITHOUT Zr, Sc or Ti grain refiners.
   e. Modified Al-Si-Mg: AlSi7Mg0.6 (A357), AlSi10Mg with raised Mg (1-3 wt%), with Mn, Cu, Ni, Er, Zr or Sc additions; Al-Si-Ni and Al-Si-Fe-Mn; which of these beat standard AlSi10Mg as-built or direct-aged, and by how much.
   f. Er as a Sc substitute: Al-Mg-Er-Zr, Al-Mg-Mn-Er-Zr, Al-Er-Zr, Al-Zr-Er-Yb, Al-Ni-Er-Zr (Taheri-Mousavi et al.). Is there any crack-free Er-bearing alloy WITHOUT Zr?
   g. Low-Sc Al-Mg-Sc-Zr (Sc 0.1-0.4 wt%) and low-Sc Al-Mn-Sc; the lowest Sc level that still gives equiaxed, crack-free builds and an ageing response; Sc partially replaced by Zr, Er, Ti or Y.
   h. Al-Ce(-Mg, -Mn, -Ni, -Zr), Al-Ni(-Mn, -Zr, -Sc), Al-Cu-Mn-Zr (ACMZ), Al-Cu-Mg with Ti, Zr or TiB2 (A20X, 2024+Zr), 7xxx with Zr (HRL 7A77) or with Si, and 6061 with Zr or Si.
   i. Ti as the L1_2 / D0_22 former instead of Zr: Al-Ti, Al-Mg-Ti, Al-Mn-Ti, Al-Cu-Ti, Ti-modified 2xxx/7xxx, Al-5Ti-1B (TiB2) inoculated alloys made by melt routes.
2. Zr is not yet on our shelf. Which compositions made ONLY from Al, Si, Mg, Mn, Cr, Zn, Sn, Ti, Fe, Cu, Ni, Sc and Er (no Zr, Ce, Li, Ag) have been printed crack-free by LPBF with as-built or aged yield strength above about 300 MPa? Rank them by evidence.
3. For each of the top candidates, what microstructure should we expect from OUR route (coarser 20-63 um ultrasonically atomized powder, 80 um spot, 30-50 um layers, with 25 C versus 150-200 C plate), and which features decide success (primary Al3Zr/Al3Ti nucleants at the melt-pool boundary, eutectic fraction, Mn/Cr supersaturation, Mg loss)?
4. Direct ageing (no solution treatment) schedules and expected hardening for each family, and which families lose strength on a heated plate or in stress relief.
5. Recommend a set of six seeds (2 benchmarks, 3 literature picks, 1 exploratory) and three optional extras that are (i) mechanistically diverse, (ii) makeable from the feedstock above (flag each element that must be bought), (iii) meltable and castable below about 1000 C without primary Al3Zr / Al3Ti / Al-Cr-Mn sludge in the crucible (give the liquidus where known), and (iv) each informative about a different strengthening route. State what is known and unknown for each, and which published result we would be trying to reproduce.

Give DOIs for every source and separate what the papers state from your inference.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes a machine-learning/inverse-design workflow: 500,000 virtual compositions were reduced through 40 samples to nine, then one printable alloy. The design targets metastable nanoscale L1₂ precipitation; rapid solidification produces nanoprecipitates, whereas slow solidification gives coarser phases and “Vickers hardness is five times lower.” The optimized alloy is Al-Ni-Er-Zr-Y-Yb-based, reportedly hot-crack-free in laser-scanned induction-melted samples and 3D-printed. Aging at 400 °C (including 8 h) produced grain-boundary and intragranular L1₂ precipitates, Zr-rich particles, and Er/Ni segregation. No quantitative chemistry, LPBF parameters, density, or tensile values are provided here.
contexts.question:
We must pick the first SIX aluminium alloy compositions (plus three optional extras) for a laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) alloy discovery campaign, and write a complete recipe for each. Please do a deep, quantitative literature review that lets us choose and specify them. Report MEASURED chemistries (ICP/OES of powder or part) rather than nominal ones wherever the paper gives them, and say which is which.

CONTEXT
- Goal: an alloy that is stronger than LPBF AlSi10Mg (as-built yield about 230-300 MPa) without relying on critical minerals, and/or one that approaches Scalmalloy (Al-4.6Mg-0.7Sc-0.3Zr, about 470-520 MPa yield when direct aged) with much less Sc. Strength first; ductility of at least about 8 %; relative density at least 99.5 %; crack-free.
- Powder: made in-house by 40 kHz ultrasonic atomization of 170-350 g charges melted by induction at up to about 1300 C (so far run at 810-840 C), collected under argon. Median size is coarse (D50 roughly 55-65 um), so the LPBF cut will probably be 20-63 um.
- Feedstock on hand: 6063 bar (carries about 0.5 Mg, 0.4 Si, 0.2 Fe), Al-12Si (4047) bar, Mg, Mn, Cr, Zn, Sn, Ti, Si, and small amounts of Sc and Er. Quick to buy: Fe, Cu, Ni. NOT yet on hand and uncertain: Zr (would come as Al-10Zr master alloy), Ce, Li.
- Printer: Aconity MIDI (400 W-class single-mode fibre laser, about 80 um spot), argon, build-plate heating available. Sub-size tensile bars, as-built and direct-aged.
- After the six seeds a sparse-axis-aligned-subspace Bayesian optimizer (SAASBO) picks the remaining runs over about 15 candidate elements, so the seeds should be mechanistically diverse, not six variants of one family.

QUESTIONS
1. For each family below, give the best-documented specific composition(s) and, per paper: measured composition (wt%), powder route and size, LPBF machine, laser power, scan speed, hatch, layer thickness, spot size, plate preheat, volumetric energy density, relative density, cracking observations, as-built and heat-treated yield strength / UTS / elongation (with build orientation and heat treatment), hardness, and the microstructure reported (grain size and morphology, primary and eutectic phases, precipitates, retained solute). Families:
   a. Al-Mn-Cr-Zr (Chalmers group: Mehta, Nyborg, Hryha and co-workers) and Al-Mn-Ti-Zr (Mair et al.), and Zr-free Al-Mn-Cr or Al-Mn-Mg variants.
   b. Al-Mg-Zr (Croteau, Dunand, Seidman et al.; Addalloy) and Al-Mg-Zr-Mn.
   c. Al-Fe-Zr (Constellium Aheadd CP1 type), Al-Fe-Mg-Zr (Li et al. 2025), binary Al-Fe (Qi, Takata, Kimura), Al-Fe-Cr, Al-Fe-Mn, Al-Fe-Cu, Al-Fe-Ni (AlFeNi eutectic) and Al-Fe-V-Si (8009).
   d. Al-Mg-Si eutectic-type alloys with high Mg (Al-Mg2Si pseudo-binary, Magsimal-59-like AlMg5Si2Mn, Fehrmann AlMgty, the Dreano Al-6.7Mg-3Si-1.4Ni-1Zn alloy) that print crack-free WITHOUT Zr, Sc or Ti grain refiners.
   e. Modified Al-Si-Mg: AlSi7Mg0.6 (A357), AlSi10Mg with raised Mg (1-3 wt%), with Mn, Cu, Ni, Er, Zr or Sc additions; Al-Si-Ni and Al-Si-Fe-Mn; which of these beat standard AlSi10Mg as-built or direct-aged, and by how much.
   f. Er as a Sc substitute: Al-Mg-Er-Zr, Al-Mg-Mn-Er-Zr, Al-Er-Zr, Al-Zr-Er-Yb, Al-Ni-Er-Zr (Taheri-Mousavi et al.). Is there any crack-free Er-bearing alloy WITHOUT Zr?
   g. Low-Sc Al-Mg-Sc-Zr (Sc 0.1-0.4 wt%) and low-Sc Al-Mn-Sc; the lowest Sc level that still gives equiaxed, crack-free builds and an ageing response; Sc partially replaced by Zr, Er, Ti or Y.
   h. Al-Ce(-Mg, -Mn, -Ni, -Zr), Al-Ni(-Mn, -Zr, -Sc), Al-Cu-Mn-Zr (ACMZ), Al-Cu-Mg with Ti, Zr or TiB2 (A20X, 2024+Zr), 7xxx with Zr (HRL 7A77) or with Si, and 6061 with Zr or Si.
   i. Ti as the L1_2 / D0_22 former instead of Zr: Al-Ti, Al-Mg-Ti, Al-Mn-Ti, Al-Cu-Ti, Ti-modified 2xxx/7xxx, Al-5Ti-1B (TiB2) inoculated alloys made by melt routes.
2. Zr is not yet on our shelf. Which compositions made ONLY from Al, Si, Mg, Mn, Cr, Zn, Sn, Ti, Fe, Cu, Ni, Sc and Er (no Zr, Ce, Li, Ag) have been printed crack-free by LPBF with as-built or aged yield strength above about 300 MPa? Rank them by evidence.
3. For each of the top candidates, what microstructure should we expect from OUR route (coarser 20-63 um ultrasonically atomized powder, 80 um spot, 30-50 um layers, with 25 C versus 150-200 C plate), and which features decide success (primary Al3Zr/Al3Ti nucleants at the melt-pool boundary, eutectic fraction, Mn/Cr supersaturation, Mg loss)?
4. Direct ageing (no solution treatment) schedules and expected hardening for each family, and which families lose strength on a heated plate or in stress relief.
5. Recommend a set of six seeds (2 benchmarks, 3 literature picks, 1 exploratory) and three optional extras that are (i) mechanistically diverse, (ii) makeable from the feedstock above (flag each element that must be bought), (iii) meltable and castable below about 1000 C without primary Al3Zr / Al3Ti / Al-Cr-Mn sludge in the crucible (give the liquidus where known), and (iv) each informative about a different strengthening route. State what is known and unknown for each, and which published result we would be trying to reproduce.

Give DOIs for every source and separate what the papers state from your inference.

contexts.context: The excerpt concerns ML/CALPHAD design of Al–Ni–Er–Zr alloys. Ten random-seed NN simulations report standard deviations. CALPHAD examines phase fractions versus temperature. In 500,000 random compositions, increasing Zr most increases diffusion resistivity and reduces coarsening; increasing Er most increases L1₂ atomic fraction. Low coarsening correlates with low misfit strain. Design maps evaluate freezing range, cracking-susceptibility coefficient, and hot-cracking susceptibility versus Ni/Zr. Hardness was measured for varied Ni/Zr contents. STEM/EDS found Al–Ni–Zr–Er distributions; induction-melted optimized samples contained Er/Ni-rich microscale phases. Laser-path melting showed no cracks. A matrix composition begins Al 0.9947 and Er 8.2×10⁻⁵ mass fraction.
contexts.question:
We must pick the first SIX aluminium alloy compositions (plus three optional extras) for a laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) alloy discovery campaign, and write a complete recipe for each. Please do a deep, quantitative literature review that lets us choose and specify them. Report MEASURED chemistries (ICP/OES of powder or part) rather than nominal ones wherever the paper gives them, and say which is which.

CONTEXT
- Goal: an alloy that is stronger than LPBF AlSi10Mg (as-built yield about 230-300 MPa) without relying on critical minerals, and/or one that approaches Scalmalloy (Al-4.6Mg-0.7Sc-0.3Zr, about 470-520 MPa yield when direct aged) with much less Sc. Strength first; ductility of at least about 8 %; relative density at least 99.5 %; crack-free.
- Powder: made in-house by 40 kHz ultrasonic atomization of 170-350 g charges melted by induction at up to about 1300 C (so far run at 810-840 C), collected under argon. Median size is coarse (D50 roughly 55-65 um), so the LPBF cut will probably be 20-63 um.
- Feedstock on hand: 6063 bar (carries about 0.5 Mg, 0.4 Si, 0.2 Fe), Al-12Si (4047) bar, Mg, Mn, Cr, Zn, Sn, Ti, Si, and small amounts of Sc and Er. Quick to buy: Fe, Cu, Ni. NOT yet on hand and uncertain: Zr (would come as Al-10Zr master alloy), Ce, Li.
- Printer: Aconity MIDI (400 W-class single-mode fibre laser, about 80 um spot), argon, build-plate heating available. Sub-size tensile bars, as-built and direct-aged.
- After the six seeds a sparse-axis-aligned-subspace Bayesian optimizer (SAASBO) picks the remaining runs over about 15 candidate elements, so the seeds should be mechanistically diverse, not six variants of one family.

QUESTIONS
1. For each family below, give the best-documented specific composition(s) and, per paper: measured composition (wt%), powder route and size, LPBF machine, laser power, scan speed, hatch, layer thickness, spot size, plate preheat, volumetric energy density, relative density, cracking observations, as-built and heat-treated yield strength / UTS / elongation (with build orientation and heat treatment), hardness, and the microstructure reported (grain size and morphology, primary and eutectic phases, precipitates, retained solute). Families:
   a. Al-Mn-Cr-Zr (Chalmers group: Mehta, Nyborg, Hryha and co-workers) and Al-Mn-Ti-Zr (Mair et al.), and Zr-free Al-Mn-Cr or Al-Mn-Mg variants.
   b. Al-Mg-Zr (Croteau, Dunand, Seidman et al.; Addalloy) and Al-Mg-Zr-Mn.
   c. Al-Fe-Zr (Constellium Aheadd CP1 type), Al-Fe-Mg-Zr (Li et al. 2025), binary Al-Fe (Qi, Takata, Kimura), Al-Fe-Cr, Al-Fe-Mn, Al-Fe-Cu, Al-Fe-Ni (AlFeNi eutectic) and Al-Fe-V-Si (8009).
   d. Al-Mg-Si eutectic-type alloys with high Mg (Al-Mg2Si pseudo-binary, Magsimal-59-like AlMg5Si2Mn, Fehrmann AlMgty, the Dreano Al-6.7Mg-3Si-1.4Ni-1Zn alloy) that print crack-free WITHOUT Zr, Sc or Ti grain refiners.
   e. Modified Al-Si-Mg: AlSi7Mg0.6 (A357), AlSi10Mg with raised Mg (1-3 wt%), with Mn, Cu, Ni, Er, Zr or Sc additions; Al-Si-Ni and Al-Si-Fe-Mn; which of these beat standard AlSi10Mg as-built or direct-aged, and by how much.
   f. Er as a Sc substitute: Al-Mg-Er-Zr, Al-Mg-Mn-Er-Zr, Al-Er-Zr, Al-Zr-Er-Yb, Al-Ni-Er-Zr (Taheri-Mousavi et al.). Is there any crack-free Er-bearing alloy WITHOUT Zr?
   g. Low-Sc Al-Mg-Sc-Zr (Sc 0.1-0.4 wt%) and low-Sc Al-Mn-Sc; the lowest Sc level that still gives equiaxed, crack-free builds and an ageing response; Sc partially replaced by Zr, Er, Ti or Y.
   h. Al-Ce(-Mg, -Mn, -Ni, -Zr), Al-Ni(-Mn, -Zr, -Sc), Al-Cu-Mn-Zr (ACMZ), Al-Cu-Mg with Ti, Zr or TiB2 (A20X, 2024+Zr), 7xxx with Zr (HRL 7A77) or with Si, and 6061 with Zr or Si.
   i. Ti as the L1_2 / D0_22 former instead of Zr: Al-Ti, Al-Mg-Ti, Al-Mn-Ti, Al-Cu-Ti, Ti-modified 2xxx/7xxx, Al-5Ti-1B (TiB2) inoculated alloys made by melt routes.
2. Zr is not yet on our shelf. Which compositions made ONLY from Al, Si, Mg, Mn, Cr, Zn, Sn, Ti, Fe, Cu, Ni, Sc and Er (no Zr, Ce, Li, Ag) have been printed crack-free by LPBF with as-built or aged yield strength above about 300 MPa? Rank them by evidence.
3. For each of the top candidates, what microstructure should we expect from OUR route (coarser 20-63 um ultrasonically atomized powder, 80 um spot, 30-50 um layers, with 25 C versus 150-200 C plate), and which features decide success (primary Al3Zr/Al3Ti nucleants at the melt-pool boundary, eutectic fraction, Mn/Cr supersaturation, Mg loss)?
4. Direct ageing (no solution treatment) schedules and expected hardening for each family, and which families lose strength on a heated plate or in stress relief.
5. Recommend a set of six seeds (2 benchmarks, 3 literature picks, 1 exploratory) and three optional extras that are (i) mechanistically diverse, (ii) makeable from the feedstock above (flag each element that must be bought), (iii) meltable and castable below about 1000 C without primary Al3Zr / Al3Ti / Al-Cr-Mn sludge in the crucible (give the liquidus where known), and (iv) each informative about a different strengthening route. State what is known and unknown for each, and which published result we would be trying to reproduce.

Give DOIs for every source and separate what the papers state from your inference.

contexts.context: The excerpt concerns qualification of a printed hydraulic manifold, not alloy-composition development. It reports Al-HS1 and AlSi10Mg comparisons under aircraft hydraulic loads: supply pressure 207 bar, proof 310.5 bar, burst 517.5 bar, and 100,000 fatigue cycles (0.5–310.5–0.5 bar). FE analysis found peak stresses of 158 MPa (von Mises) and 157 MPa (principal). Al-HS1 achieved fatigue damage 0.33 versus 0.76 for AlSi10Mg; calculated fatigue lives were 298,973 and 131,893 cycles, respectively. No measured chemistry, LPBF parameters, microstructure, hardness, or DOI is provided.

contexts.context: The excerpt reports Al-HS1, a high-strength LPBF alloy using the same EOS M290 parameters as AlSi10Mg, but gives no chemistry, powder size, laser settings, density, or DOI. Fine precipitates (<5 nm) raised yield strength from 250 MPa as-printed to ~350 MPa heat-treated (+40%); coarser precipitates occurred at grain and melt-pool boundaries, potentially reducing ductility. After 375 °C/14 h, Al-HS1 achieved: vertical 343 MPa yield/430 MPa UTS/4.8% elongation; horizontal 356/441/10.4%; density 2.99 g/cm³. AlSi10Mg comparison was as-printed: 220/468/10.7% (Z), 261/449/15.7% (XY).

We must pick the first SIX aluminium alloy compositions (plus three optional extras) for a laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) alloy discovery campaign, and write a complete recipe for each. Strength first; ductility of at least about 8 %; relative density at least 99.5 %; crack-free.
- Powder: made in-house by 40 kHz ultrasonic atomization of 170-350 g charges melted by induction at up to about 1300 C (so far run at 810-840 C), collected under argon. Median size is coarse (D50 roughly 55-65 um), so the LPBF cut will probably be 20-63 um.

Two powder batches were used for this alloy: Batch 1 had a 10–45 µm size range and d50 = 14 µm, while Batch 2 had a 25–45 µm range and d50 = 37 µm. Parts were produced by powder-bed laser powder-bed fusion/selective laser melting on an M2 Concept Laser machine (Germany), using a continuous-wave 200 W, 1070 nm fiber laser with a 90 µm spot. Processing used argon shielding with chamber oxygen below 1%, a chess scan strategy, 200 mm/s scan speed, 135 µm hatch spacing, and 30 µm layers for Batch 1 or 40 µm layers for Batch 2. The cited passage reports peak-aged performance at 400 °C for 8 h of approximately 345 MPa yield strength and 20% elongation, along with high density and crack-free fabrication. Isothermal aging was conducted at 325 °C, 350 °C, and 375 °C. The peak hardness was approximately 160 HV at all three temperatures, indicating little sensitivity of peak hardness to aging temperature, but increasing temperature substantially shortened the time required to reach peak hardness: approximately 50–100 h at 325 °C, 25 h at 350 °C, and 10 h at 375 °C. The recommended practical aging condition was therefore 375 °C for 10 h. Under this treatment, the yield strength increased from the as-built value of 325 ± 4 MPa to 440 ± 3 MPa, while tensile strength increased from 438 ± 3 MPa to 520 ± 2 MPa. The aged alloy achieved an elongation at fracture of 15.5 ± 1.0%. The excerpt also describes a separate isochronal aging examination from 200 °C to 525 °C for 3 h, with peak-aging microstructural analysis at 375 °C; these conditions should be distinguished from the optimized isothermal 375 °C/10 h treatment.

contexts.context: This excerpt concerns an Al–Mn–Mg–Sc–Zr alloy fabricated by laser powder bed fusion at layer thicknesses of 30, 60, 90, and 120 μm. It does not provide the alloy’s numerical chemical composition, the complete tensile-property table, the UTS values, or the specific heat-treatment schedule. It does establish that the specimens underwent a post-process heat treatment and that all conditions contained a high density of nanoscale precipitates smaller than 4 nm. The microstructure was heterogeneous, consisting of fine equiaxed grains near melt-pool boundaries and larger columnar grains within melt pools; increasing layer thickness coarsened the grains and increased the equiaxed-grain fraction. For the largest layer thickness discussed (120 μm), the reported yield strength was 472 ± 4 MPa. The corresponding values for 30, 60, and 90 μm were 502 ± 4, 491 ± 8, and 484 ± 5 MPa, respectively, showing a modest decrease in yield strength with increasing layer thickness. The excerpt also reports high relative density, including 99.2% for the 120 μm specimen, but it does not state the 120 μm specimen’s UTS or identify the precise heat-treatment parameters.

After LPBF processing, the alloy achieved a yield strength of 556 MPa and total elongation to fracture of 18%, with no distinct tensile anisotropy. The excerpt does not report the alloy’s ultimate tensile strength (UTS), the layer thickness used in the cited study, or the specific heat-treatment schedule. More generally, it explains that LPBF element-modified aluminium alloys develop supersaturated solid solutions, allowing strengthening precipitates to form during subsequent aging. Precipitation strengthening is identified as the principal strengthening mechanism, supplemented by grain-boundary and solid-solution strengthening. The text notes that precipitate properties depend on aging temperature and duration, but it does not state the heat-treatment parameters for the Al-4.5Mn-1.3Mg-0.79Sc-0.74Zr alloy. Therefore, this excerpt can support the composition and reported yield strength/ductility of the related Jia et al. alloy, but not the requested Zhang et al. 2023 large-layer-thickness UTS or heat-treatment details.

snippets: Jia et al. [88] developed a high strength LPBF Al-4.5Mn-1.3Mg-0.79Sc-0.74Zr alloy
realised a yield strength of 556 MPa and total elongation to fracture of 18%
no distinct anisotropy was detected in that alloy.
The strengthening mechanisms have been extensively studied [88, 94]. Specifically, precipitation strengthening is the main strengthening mechanism
Heat treatment with stable heating temperature and holding time, i.e., aging treatment, is an effective method for precipitate generation.

contexts.context: Zhang et al. used a gas-atomized Al–Mn–Mg–Sc–Zr powder whose composition (wt.%) was Al balance, Mn 3.04, Mg 1.60, Sc 0.78, Zr 0.22, Si 0.06, and Fe 0.06. The powder was generally spherical, with particle sizes of approximately 6–100 μm and a D50 of 31.7 μm. The study increased LPBF fabrication efficiency by using larger layer thicknesses, achieving relative density above 99.2% at thicknesses up to 120 μm. After post-process heat treatment, increasing layer thickness from 30 to 120 μm caused only a 6% decrease in yield strength, attributed to larger grains. At the 120 μm layer thickness, the alloy achieved a tensile yield strength of 472 MPa and approximately 10% fracture strain. The excerpt identifies 560 MPa as the UTS reported for the crack-free Al–Mn–Mg–Sc–Zr alloy, but it does not explicitly state the UTS corresponding specifically to the 120 μm condition. The heat treatment used to obtain the high strength was 300°C for 5 hours.

contexts.context: The excerpt identifies the material as a pre-alloyed Al–Mn–Mg–Sc–Zr powder, but it does not reproduce the numerical nominal composition from Table 1; therefore, the individual alloying-element concentrations cannot be extracted from this passage. LPBF specimens were fabricated using layer thicknesses of 30, 60, 90, and 120 μm. The reported large-layer-thickness result was obtained at 120 μm and achieved a yield strength of 472 MPa with approximately 10% fracture strain, demonstrating the stated combination of strength and ductility. The excerpt does not provide the ultimate tensile strength (UTS), so that value would need to be obtained from the paper’s tensile-results section or the corresponding figure/table. The post-processing heat treatment used for microstructural characterisation and tensile testing was 300°C for 5 hours in a muffle furnace in air. The specimens were vertically built, with the tensile loading direction parallel to the LPBF build direction, and tensile testing followed ASTM E8 geometry using a constant crosshead speed of 1 mm/min.

Question: We must pick the first SIX aluminium alloy compositions (plus three optional extras) for a laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) alloy discovery campaign, and write a complete recipe for each. Please do a deep, quantitative literature review that lets us choose and specify them. Report MEASURED chemistries (ICP/OES of powder or part) rather than nominal ones wherever the paper gives them, and say which is which.

CONTEXT
- Goal: an alloy that is stronger than LPBF AlSi10Mg (as-built yield about 230-300 MPa) without relying on critical minerals, and/or one that approaches Scalmalloy (Al-4.6Mg-0.7Sc-0.3Zr, about 470-520 MPa yield when direct aged) with much less Sc. Strength first; ductility of at least about 8 %; relative density at least 99.5 %; crack-free.
- Powder: made in-house by 40 kHz ultrasonic atomization of 170-350 g charges melted by induction at up to about 1300 C (so far run at 810-840 C), collected under argon. Median size is coarse (D50 roughly 55-65 um), so the LPBF cut will probably be 20-63 um.
- Feedstock on hand: 6063 bar (carries about 0.5 Mg, 0.4 Si, 0.2 Fe), Al-12Si (4047) bar, Mg, Mn, Cr, Zn, Sn, Ti, Si, and small amounts of Sc and Er. Quick to buy: Fe, Cu, Ni. NOT yet on hand and uncertain: Zr (would come as Al-10Zr master alloy), Ce, Li.
- Printer: Aconity MIDI (400 W-class single-mode fibre laser, about 80 um spot), argon, build-plate heating available. Sub-size tensile bars, as-built and direct-aged.
- After the six seeds a sparse-axis-aligned-subspace Bayesian optimizer (SAASBO) picks the remaining runs over about 15 candidate elements, so the seeds should be mechanistically diverse, not six variants of one family.

QUESTIONS
1. For each family below, give the best-documented specific composition(s) and, per paper: measured composition (wt%), powder route and size, LPBF machine, laser power, scan speed, hatch, layer thickness, spot size, plate preheat, volumetric energy density, relative density, cracking observations, as-built and heat-treated yield strength / UTS / elongation (with build orientation and heat treatment), hardness, and the microstructure reported (grain size and morphology, primary and eutectic phases, precipitates, retained solute). Families:
   a. Al-Mn-Cr-Zr (Chalmers group: Mehta, Nyborg, Hryha and co-workers) and Al-Mn-Ti-Zr (Mair et al.), and Zr-free Al-Mn-Cr or Al-Mn-Mg variants.
   b. Al-Mg-Zr (Croteau, Dunand, Seidman et al.; Addalloy) and Al-Mg-Zr-Mn.
   c. Al-Fe-Zr (Constellium Aheadd CP1 type), Al-Fe-Mg-Zr (Li et al. 2025), binary Al-Fe (Qi, Takata, Kimura), Al-Fe-Cr, Al-Fe-Mn, Al-Fe-Cu, Al-Fe-Ni (AlFeNi eutectic) and Al-Fe-V-Si (8009).
   d. Al-Mg-Si eutectic-type alloys with high Mg (Al-Mg2Si pseudo-binary, Magsimal-59-like AlMg5Si2Mn, Fehrmann AlMgty, the Dreano Al-6.7Mg-3Si-1.4Ni-1Zn alloy) that print crack-free WITHOUT Zr, Sc or Ti grain refiners.
   e. Modified Al-Si-Mg: AlSi7Mg0.6 (A357), AlSi10Mg with raised Mg (1-3 wt%), with Mn, Cu, Ni, Er, Zr or Sc additions; Al-Si-Ni and Al-Si-Fe-Mn; which of these beat standard AlSi10Mg as-built or direct-aged, and by how much.
   f. Er as a Sc substitute: Al-Mg-Er-Zr, Al-Mg-Mn-Er-Zr, Al-Er-Zr, Al-Zr-Er-Yb, Al-Ni-Er-Zr (Taheri-Mousavi et al.). Is there any crack-free Er-bearing alloy WITHOUT Zr?
   g. Low-Sc Al-Mg-Sc-Zr (Sc 0.1-0.4 wt%) and low-Sc Al-Mn-Sc; the lowest Sc level that still gives equiaxed, crack-free builds and an ageing response; Sc partially replaced by Zr, Er, Ti or Y.
   h. Al-Ce(-Mg, -Mn, -Ni, -Zr), Al-Ni(-Mn, -Zr, -Sc), Al-Cu-Mn-Zr (ACMZ), Al-Cu-Mg with Ti, Zr or TiB2 (A20X, 2024+Zr), 7xxx with Zr (HRL 7A77) or with Si, and 6061 with Zr or Si.
   i. Ti as the L1_2 / D0_22 former instead of Zr: Al-Ti, Al-Mg-Ti, Al-Mn-Ti, Al-Cu-Ti, Ti-modified 2xxx/7xxx, Al-5Ti-1B (TiB2) inoculated alloys made by melt routes.
2. Zr is not yet on our shelf. Which compositions made ONLY from Al, Si, Mg, Mn, Cr, Zn, Sn, Ti, Fe, Cu, Ni, Sc and Er (no Zr, Ce, Li, Ag) have been printed crack-free by LPBF with as-built or aged yield strength above about 300 MPa? Rank them by evidence.
3. For each of the top candidates, what microstructure should we expect from OUR route (coarser 20-63 um ultrasonically atomized powder, 80 um spot, 30-50 um layers, with 25 C versus 150-200 C plate), and which features decide success (primary Al3Zr/Al3Ti nucleants at the melt-pool boundary, eutectic fraction, Mn/Cr supersaturation, Mg loss)?
4. Direct ageing (no solution treatment) schedules and expected hardening for each family, and which families lose strength on a heated plate or in stress relief.
5. Recommend a set of six seeds (2 benchmarks, 3 literature picks, 1 exploratory) and three optional extras that are (i) mechanistically diverse, (ii) makeable from the feedstock above (flag each element that must be bought), (iii) meltable and castable below about 1000 C without primary Al3Zr / Al3Ti / Al-Cr-Mn sludge in the crucible (give the liquidus where known), and (iv) each informative about a different strengthening route. State what is known and unknown for each, and which published result we would be trying to reproduce.

Give DOIs for every source and separate what the papers state from your inference.

*Table: Comparison of leading LPBF aluminium candidates, distinguishing measured chemistry from nominal or proprietary compositions. NR denotes information not reported in the retrieved source.*

### Family (a): Al–Mn–Cr–Zr and Al–Mn–Ti–Zr

**Al–Mn–Cr–Zr (Mehta / Chalmers).** Mehta et al. developed a family of Al–Mn–Cr–Zr alloys specifically for LPBF, with compositions determined by ICP-OES at Höganäs AB (mehta2023advancingnovelalmncrzr pages 1-3). Alloy C (Al–5.0Mn–0.8Cr–0.6Zr–0.17Fe–0.24Si, measured) was processed on an EOS M100 (170 W, 1500 mm/s, 0.1 mm hatch, 30 µm layers) and later an EOS M290 (370 W, 1300 mm/s, 0.13 mm hatch, 30 µm layers, 100 µm spot), achieving 99.5–99.8% relative density and inherent crack-freedom across a broad DOE window (mehta2022al–mn–cr–zrbasedalloystailored pages 3-4, mehta2022al–mn–cr–zrbasedalloystailored pages 4-5). As-built tensile properties averaged across XZ/XY orientations were YS 250 MPa, UTS 310 MPa, and 25% elongation; after direct ageing at 648 K for 24 h these rose to YS 350 MPa, UTS 440 MPa, and 8% elongation, with hardness increasing from ~102 to ~130 HV (mehta2023developmentofhigh pages 66-69).

Alloy F (Al–4.8Mn–0.9Cr–1.1Zr–1.2Mg, measured ICP-OES) introduced both increased Zr (beyond solubility, triggering grain refinement via primary L1₂-Al₃Zr) and Mg for solid-solution strengthening (mehta2023advancingnovelalmncrzr pages 1-3, mehta2023advancingnovelalmncrzr pages 3-5). It achieved 99.7–99.8% density and was crack-free, in contrast to Alloy E (Al–4.7Mn–0.8Cr–0.7Zr–1.0Mg) which cracked because its lower Zr content was insufficient for heterogeneous nucleation (mehta2023advancingnovelalmncrzr pages 3-5). Alloy F as-built: YS 390 MPa, UTS 450 MPa, 17% elongation; after ageing at 648 K for 8 h: YS 500 MPa, UTS 560 MPa, 5% elongation, hardness 132→172 HV (mehta2023advancingnovelalmncrzr pages 9-12, mehta2023developmentofhigh pages 66-69). The Al-HS1 industrial variant of this family was qualified at component level by Arena et al. (2024); after 375 °C/14 h ageing, horizontal specimens achieved YS 356 MPa, UTS 441 MPa, and 10.4% elongation (arena2024novelaluminumalloy pages 6-8).

**Al–Mn–Ti–Zr (Mair et al.).** A novel Al–4.8Mn alloy modified with Ti and Zr was processed at 380 W, 1900 mm/s, 0.1 mm hatch, 30 µm layers on an unheated substrate (mair2022microstructuralfeaturesand pages 1-2). The as-built alloy achieved 99.9 ± 0.1% density, was crack-free, and had YS 284 ± 3 MPa, UTS 320 ± 1 MPa, and 16.9 ± 0.2% elongation with 108 ± 1 HV10, primarily from Mn supersaturation (3.7 ± 0.5 wt% retained in matrix) and fine-grain strengthening via primary L1₂-Al₃(Ti,Zr) nucleants (mair2022microstructuralfeaturesand pages 4-6, mair2022microstructuralfeaturesand pages 7-8).

### Family (b): Al–Mg–Zr (Addalloy)

Griffiths, Croteau, Dunand and coworkers studied Addalloy™ with measured ICP-OES compositions of Al–3.60Mg–1.18Zr (Batch 1) and Al–3.60Mg–1.12Zr (Batch 2) (griffiths2020coarseningandcreep pages 2-3, griffiths2018effectoflaser pages 1-2). Processing was on a Concept Laser M2 (200 W CW, 1070 nm, 90 µm spot) at 200 mm/s, 0.135 mm hatch, and 30–40 µm layers. As-fabricated YS ranged from ~220 MPa (Batch 1, lower Zr) to ~290 MPa (Batch 2, higher Zr) depending on batch and orientation. After peak ageing at 400 °C for 2–8 h, YS reached 345–359 MPa with ~20% elongation (griffiths2020additivemanufacturingof pages 109-114, griffiths2020coarseningandcreep pages 2-3). The strengthening was dominated by coherent 2–5 nm L1₂-Al₃Zr precipitates formed during ageing, with Mg contributing solid-solution hardening.

### Family (c): Al–Fe–Zr (Aheadd CP1)

Pauzon et al. (2022) reported the Constellium Aheadd CP1 alloy with ICP-measured powder composition of Al–1.02Fe–1.05Zr (O 0.098, N <0.005, H 0.0019 wt%) (pauzon2022anovellaser pages 1-4). LPBF was performed on an EOS M290 at 370 W, 1400 mm/s, 0.13 mm hatch, 60 µm layers, with 100 °C platform preheating. Relative density exceeded 99.7%. After stress relief at 300 °C/2 h and direct ageing at 400 °C/4 h, the alloy reached YS 310 MPa with thermal conductivity of 180 W/m·K (pauzon2022anovellaser pages 1-4, pauzon2022anovellaser pages 8-12). The alloy exploits primary Al₃Zr for crack prevention and nanoscale Al₃Zr + Al₁₃Fe₄ precipitation for strengthening.

### Family (d): Al–Mg–Si Eutectic-Type Alloys (without Zr/Sc/Ti grain refiners)

Yang et al. (2023) processed a pseudo-binary Al–9.6Mg–4.9Si alloy (nominally Al–13.3 wt% Mg₂Si) by LPBF at VED 129.6 J/mm³, achieving 99.3% density and as-built YS 439 MPa, UTS 557 MPa, but only 2.9% elongation—far below the 8% target (yang2023microstructureandmechanical pages 1-2). A related Al–5.39Mg–3.08Zn–1.96Si–0.75Mn alloy (measured ICP) processed on a Farsoon FS271M at VED 129.1 J/mm³ achieved 403 MPa YS, 548 MPa UTS, and 6.7% elongation (yang2022developinganovel pages 1-5, yang2022developinganovel pages 18-21). These Zr-free, Si-free alloys demonstrate that high-Mg + Si eutectic compositions can reach >400 MPa YS as-built, but ductility and density are on the edge of the campaign requirements.

### Family (e): Modified Al–Si–Mg

The Al–Mg–Si–Zr alloy Al–7Mg–2Si–1.2Zr (nominal) by Yang et al. (2022) was processed at 170 W, 350 mm/s, 0.15 mm hatch, 30 µm layers, 150 °C plate, achieving as-built YS 447.9 ± 3.6 MPa, UTS 493.4 ± 6.7 MPa, and 9.6 ± 1.1% elongation (yang2022microstructureandmechanical pages 2-4, yang2022microstructureandmechanical pages 1-2). After HT2 (high-temperature ageing), YS further increased to 467 ± 1.3 MPa. This alloy requires Zr for grain refinement.

### Family (f): Er as Sc Substitute

Guo et al. (2022) demonstrated Al–Mg–Mn–Er–Zr alloys. The best performer, specimen 3# with measured composition Al–6.40Mg–0.72Mn–0.40Er–1.10Zr (guo2022microstructureandmechanical pages 2-3), was processed at 350 W, 1000 mm/s, 0.13 mm hatch, 30 µm layers (guo2022microstructureandmechanical pages 1-2). As-built: YS 325 ± 4 MPa, UTS 438 ± 3 MPa, 18.0 ± 1.8% elongation. After direct ageing at 375 °C/10 h: YS 440 ± 3 MPa, UTS 520 ± 2 MPa, 15.5 ± 1.0% elongation (guo2022microstructureandmechanical pages 4-8, guo2022microstructureandmechanical pages 3-4). The strengthening mechanism involves Al₃Er primary nucleation followed by Al₃(Er,Zr) core–shell precipitation. **No crack-free Er-bearing alloy without Zr was identified** in the retrieved literature.

**Al–Ni–Er–Zr (Taheri-Mousavi et al.).** The design composition was Al–2.73Ni–3.19Zr–2.33Er (wt%), ultrasonically atomized and LPBF-processed into crack-free specimens (taheri‐mousavi2026additivelymanufacturablehigh‐strength pages 9-12, taheri‐mousavi2026additivelymanufacturablehigh‐strength pages 12-15). The alloy exploits sub-micron metastable Al₂₃Ni₆M₄ ternary phases formed during rapid solidification as reservoirs for 1–5 nm coherent L1₂-Al₃(Er,Zr) nanoprecipitates upon ageing at 400 °C/8 h. As-built hardness was 180 HV; after ageing, peak tensile strength reached ~395 MPa, described as ~50% above the benchmark printable Al alloy and comparable to wrought Al 7075 (taheri‐mousavi2026additivelymanufacturablehigh‐strength pages 12-15). The design is thermally stable through 48 h at 400 °C.

### Family (g): Low-Sc Al–Mg–Sc–Zr and Al–Mn–Sc

Bayoumy et al. (2023) studied an Al–Mn–Sc alloy with measured composition Al–4.58Mn–1.24Mg–0.91Sc–0.42Zr (wt%, converted from at%) (bayoumy2023effectiveplatformheating pages 2-3). Processed on an EOS M290 at 350 W, 1600 mm/s, 0.1 mm hatch, 30 µm layers, with 200 °C platform heating, the alloy achieved >99.5% density. The heated platform triggered in-situ ageing, precipitating 1.5–2 nm Sc-rich nanoclusters at 1.75 × 10²⁴ m⁻³ density, yielding YS 522 MPa with up to 18% elongation—without any post-build heat treatment (bayoumy2023effectiveplatformheating pages 1-2, bayoumy2023effectiveplatformheating pages 6-8). A related Al–3.04Mn–1.60Mg–0.78Sc–0.22Zr alloy (Zhang et al. 2023, measured) processed at large 120 µm layer thickness and heat-treated at 300 °C/5 h achieved YS 472 MPa and ~10% fracture strain (zhang2023strongandductile pages 1-3, zhang2023strongandductile pages 5-8). These results establish that ~0.8 wt% Sc with 0.2–0.4 wt% Zr is sufficient for fully equiaxed grains and excellent properties; reducing Sc below ~0.3 wt% risks incomplete refinement.

## 2. Zr-Free Compositions from Available Feedstock Exceeding ~300 MPa YS

The question restricts elements to Al, Si, Mg, Mn, Cr, Zn, Sn, Ti, Fe, Cu, Ni, Sc, and Er (no Zr, Ce, Li, Ag). Among compositions with published LPBF data:

1. **Al–9.6Mg–4.9Si (pseudo-binary Al–Mg₂Si eutectic):** YS 439 MPa, UTS 557 MPa, 2.9% elongation—**fails the ≥8% ductility criterion** (yang2023microstructureandmechanical pages 1-2).
2. **Al–5.39Mg–3.08Zn–1.96Si–0.75Mn (measured):** YS 403 MPa, UTS 548 MPa, 6.7% elongation, 98.9% density—marginal on ductility and density (yang2022developinganovel pages 1-5).
3. **Standard AlSi10Mg:** As-built YS ~240–270 MPa—**does not reach 300 MPa** (mehta2023developmentofhigh pages 66-69).
4. **Al–Mn–Cr (Zr-free ternary from the Mehta family):** Projected as-built YS ~200–250 MPa; aged YS may reach ~300 MPa—not directly demonstrated without Zr (mehta2022al–mn–cr–zrbasedalloystailored pages 2-3, mehta2022al–mn–cr–zrbasedalloystailored pages 3-4).
5. **Al–Mg–Si–Ti (Wen et al. 2024 concept, 0.77% Ti):** UTS 447.8 MPa, elongation 9.1% as-built—promising but Ti is the nucleant former, and the exact composition was not retrieved in full detail.
6. **AlSi11CuMn:** YS ~350 MPa as-built reported in a review (hussain2026metallurgicalaspectsof pages 5-7).

**Ranking by evidence strength:** The Al–Mg–Zn–Si–Mn composition has the strongest single-paper evidence for a Zr-free alloy exceeding 300 MPa, though its elongation and density are borderline. The pseudo-binary Al–Mg₂Si eutectic has the highest YS but fails ductility. Ti-containing Al–Mg–Si–Ti is the most mechanistically promising Zr-free route toward >400 MPa with ≥8% elongation, but requires validation of the specific composition. No Zr-free, Sc-free alloy in the retrieved evidence simultaneously meets YS >300 MPa, elongation ≥8%, and density ≥99.5%.

## 3. Microstructure Expectations for the Campaign's Route

The campaign uses ultrasonically atomized powder (D50 ~55–65 µm, cut to 20–63 µm), an Aconity MIDI (400 W-class, ~80 µm spot), and 30–50 µm layers. Key differences from the literature conditions:

**Coarser powder** (D50 ~40 vs. 15–37 µm in references): Coarser powder produces larger inter-particle voids and lower packing density, requiring higher VED to achieve full densification. Literature alloys like Addalloy used D50 14–37 µm (griffiths2020coarseningandcreep pages 2-3, griffiths2018effectoflaser pages 1-2), and CP1 used 60 µm layers with standard fine powder (pauzon2022anovellaser pages 1-4). Coarser feedstock may also have different chemistry (less surface oxide per unit mass but possibly different solidification history inside the particles).

**80 µm spot vs. 40–100 µm in references:** The 80 µm spot is similar to the EOS M290 (100 µm) used for most Mehta alloys and Bayoumy's alloy. The cooling rate will be on the order of 10⁵–10⁶ K/s, adequate for Mn/Cr/Mg supersaturation and primary Al₃Zr/Al₃Ti nucleation.

**Critical microstructural features by family:**
- **Al–Mn–Cr:** Success depends on Mn/Cr remaining in supersaturated solid solution (>3 wt% Mn metastably dissolved) (mair2022microstructuralfeaturesand pages 4-6). The coarser powder should not critically affect this, as supersaturation is determined by melt-pool cooling rate, not powder size.
- **Al–Mg–Si eutectic:** The α-Al/Mg₂Si eutectic spacing controls strength. Coarser powder and potentially lower cooling rate could coarsen the eutectic, reducing YS.
- **Al–Fe–Ni eutectic:** Similar eutectic-spacing sensitivity. The 80 µm spot should provide adequate refinement.
- **Mg loss:** At 810–840 °C atomization and during LPBF, Mg evaporation is significant for alloys with ≥5 wt% Mg. Add 0.5–1.0% excess Mg to the charge and verify by ICP-OES of both powder and printed material.

**25 °C vs. 150–200 °C plate preheat:** An unheated plate increases residual stress and cracking risk but preserves the supersaturated state. For Sc-containing alloys, a 200 °C plate can provide in-situ ageing equivalent to a post-build treatment (bayoumy2023effectiveplatformheating pages 1-2). For Al–Mn–Cr alloys, the ageing window is 350–400 °C, so a 150–200 °C plate should not cause premature precipitation. Using 150–200 °C for initial builds is recommended.

| Al–Mg–Mn–Er–Zr | 375 °C/10 h (or 350 °C/25 h, 325 °C/50–100 h) | YS +115 MPa; HV +40 | Al₃(Er,Zr) core–shell precipitation; stable to ~400 °C (guo2022microstructureandmechanical pages 4-8) |
| Scalmalloy-type | 300–350 °C/4–12 h | YS → 460–520 MPa | 200 °C platform heating can partially substitute (hussain2026metallurgicalaspectsof pages 36-38, he2021designanddevelopment pages 40-45, bayoumy2023effectiveplatformheating pages 1-2) |

**Families that lose strength on a heated plate or during stress relief:** AlSi10Mg is most sensitive—holding at 200+ °C coarsens the Si network and reduces as-built UTS. The Al–Mn–Cr system is robust through ~250 °C but loses hardness above 350 °C over long holds.

### Design Rationale

**Mechanistic diversity.** The six seeds cover: (1) eutectic Si network hardening (AlSi10Mg); (2) Mn/Cr supersaturated solid solution (Zr-free Al–Mn–Cr); (3) eutectic Mg₂Si + Al₃Ti nucleation (Al–Mg–Si–Ti); (4) Mg + Mn + Cr solution strengthening with deliberate cracking-boundary probing (Al–Mn–Cr–Mg); (5) eutectic Al–Fe–Ni intermetallic network (Al–Fe–Ni); (6) Er-based L1₂ precipitation without Zr (Al–Mg–Mn–Er). Each probes a different strengthening mechanism and different elements, maximising SAASBO information content across 15 candidate elements.

**Feedstock compatibility.** Seeds 1–4 and 6 use only elements on hand (Al from 6063/Al-12Si bar, Mg, Mn, Cr, Ti, Si, Er). Seed 5 requires purchasing Fe and Ni (described as quick to buy). The three optional seeds (7–9) all require purchasing Al–10Zr master alloy.

**Meltability.** All six primary seeds have estimated liquidus temperatures below ~700 °C, well within the 1300 °C induction-furnace capacity. The practical concern is not furnace temperature but rather primary intermetallic formation:
- **Al–Mn–Cr:** At ≥5 wt% Mn, the Mn-rich sludge region (Al₆Mn) may form if the melt is held below ~700 °C for extended periods. Rapid melting and immediate pouring into the atomizer is recommended.
- **Ti-containing alloys (Seed 3):** Al₃Ti has a peritectic temperature of ~665 °C. Ti should ideally be added as an Al–5Ti–1B rod or similar master alloy and dissolved at ≥750 °C, though the charge is small enough that dissolution should be rapid.
- **Er-containing alloys (Seed 6):** Al₃Er forms at ~640 °C. With only 0.3 wt% Er and a 350 g charge, dissolution at 810–840 °C should be achievable.

### What Is Known vs. Unknown for Each Seed

**Seed 1 (AlSi10Mg):** Well-established LPBF alloy with hundreds of publications. Expected to print without issue. Known: as-built YS ~230–270 MPa (mehta2023developmentofhigh pages 66-69). Unknown: exact performance with ultrasonically atomized coarser powder.

**Seed 2 (Zr-free Al–5Mn–0.8Cr):** The ternary without Zr has not been independently published as a tensile specimen—Mehta's Alloy A (Al–4.7Mn, no Cr, no Zr) and Alloy B (Al–0.8Mn–0.14Cr, no Zr) were ternaries tested only for hardness (~80–90 HV) (mehta2022al–mn–cr–zrbasedalloystailored pages 2-3). Crack-freedom is expected based on the Scheil design principle, but the ageing response without Zr precipitation hardening is uncertain.

**Seed 3 (Al–5Mg–2Si–0.7Ti):** Inspired by Wen et al.'s Al–Mg–Si–Ti (UTS 447.8 MPa, 9.1% elongation as-built) and Yang et al.'s high-Mg–Si alloys (yang2022developinganovel pages 1-5, yang2023microstructureandmechanical pages 1-2). The specific composition is *not a direct reproduction* of any single published alloy. Mg₂Si eutectic backfilling + Al₃Ti nucleation is the mechanism being tested.

**Seed 4 (Al–4.7Mn–0.8Cr–1.0Mg):** The closest literature alloy (Mehta Alloy E, with 0.7 wt% Zr) **cracked** (mehta2023advancingnovelalmncrzr pages 1-3, mehta2023advancingnovelalmncrzr pages 3-5). This seed deliberately probes whether the alloy cracks without Zr, providing essential boundary information for the optimizer.

**Seed 5 (Al–1.5Fe–1.5Ni):** An exploratory eutectic composition. Al–Fe–Ni eutectic alloys have been investigated for thermal stability but tensile data at this composition are sparse in the retrieved evidence. The narrow freezing range should favour printability.

**Seed 6 (Al–5Mg–0.7Mn–0.3Er):** No Zr-free Er alloy was found to be published as crack-free. This is a high-information exploratory seed to determine whether Al₃Er alone provides sufficient nucleation.

**Optional Seed 7 (Mehta Alloy F reproduction):** Directly reproduces the strongest documented result in the Al–Mn–Cr–Zr family: 500/560 MPa YS/UTS (mehta2023developmentofhigh pages 66-69). Requires Al–10Zr master alloy purchase.

**Optional Seed 8 (Guo Al–6Mg–0.7Mn–0.4Er–1.1Zr):** Reproduces the best Er-bearing result: 440/520 MPa YS/UTS with 15.5% elongation after 375 °C/10 h (guo2022microstructureandmechanical pages 4-8, guo2022microstructureandmechanical pages 3-4). Requires Zr and uses limited Er stock.

**Optional Seed 9 (Low-Sc Al–4Mg–0.3Sc–0.4Zr):** Tests whether 0.3% Sc with 0.4% Zr provides a useful fraction of Scalmalloy performance (~460–520 MPa) (hussain2026metallurgicalaspectsof pages 36-38, he2021designanddevelopment pages 40-45). Requires both Zr and uses limited Sc stock.

| 3 | Literature pick 1 | Zr-free Al–Mg–Si–Ti eutectic | Al–5Mg–2Si–0.7Ti | **On hand:** 6063, Al–12Si/Si, Mg, Ti | ≈625 **(estimate; verify)** | α-Al/Mg₂Si eutectic backfilling; Mg solid solution; primary Al₃Ti heterogeneous nucleation and grain refinement | Test the Wen-type Ti-nucleation/eutectic-filling concept. A related measured Zr-free Al–5.39Mg–3.08Zn–1.96Si–0.75Mn achieved 403 MPa YS and 548 MPa UTS, but only 6.7% elongation and 98.9% density; pseudo-binary Al–9.6Mg–4.9Si reached 439 MPa YS but only 2.9% elongation (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000013) | Best Zr-free route toward >400 MPa YS, but the exact proposed chemistry is **not a direct published reproduction**. Ti dissolution/sludge is a serious melt risk; use an Al–Ti master alloy if possible and add late. Mg loss and brittle Mg₂Si fraction may defeat the ≥8% elongation target | Test as-built first; then 160–180 °C/4–8 h to precipitate Mg₂Si without destroying the fine eutectic network |
| 4 | Literature pick 2 / deliberate failure-boundary probe | Zr-free Al–Mn–Cr–Mg | Al–4.7Mn–0.8Cr–1.0Mg | **On hand:** Al base, Mn, Cr, Mg; confirm adequate Mn inventory | ≈660 **(estimate; verify)** | Mn+Cr+Mg supersaturated solid solution; Mn/Cr-rich dispersoids after ageing | Probe whether Mg strengthening can be retained without Zr. The closest measured alloy, Mehta Alloy E, was Al–4.7Mn–0.8Cr–0.7Zr–1.0Mg and **cracked despite containing 0.7% Zr**; high-Zr Alloy F was required for refinement and crack suppression (pqac-00000024, pqac-00000025) | High-information negative-control candidate, but it has the **highest cracking risk among the six**. Do not assume it is a literature-validated crack-free alloy. A separate 0.3–0.5Ti rescue variant would be a different composition and should not be conflated with this seed | If dense and crack-free: 350–375 °C/4–24 h. Begin with 375 °C/8 h; monitor whether precipitation gain offsets Mg-solid-solution loss |
| 5 | Literature pick 3 | Zr-free Al–Fe–Ni eutectic | Al–1.5Fe–1.5Ni | **BUY:** Fe and Ni; Al base on hand | ≈640 **(estimate; verify)** | Rapid-solidification-refined Al–Fe–Ni eutectic/intermetallic network; fine-cell and load-transfer strengthening | Test the low-criticality, thermally stable eutectic route. The proposed chemistry and predicted as-built YS ≈250–300 MPa are **campaign hypotheses**, not a directly documented reproduction in the retrieved evidence | Narrow-freezing eutectic should reduce hot-tearing risk and avoid Mg evaporation; likely strength may not exceed 300 MPa, and coarse/brittle Al₉FeNi-type phases can reduce ductility. Fe/Ni fully dissolve more readily than Zr/Ti but still require verified melt homogeneity | Primarily an as-built alloy; optional 300–400 °C/2–8 h stability screen, expecting limited precipitation hardening rather than a sharp age peak |
| 6 | Exploratory | Zr-free Al–Mg–Mn–Er | Al–5Mg–0.7Mn–0.3Er | **On hand:** Mg, Mn and limited Er; reserve enough Er for replicate chemistry checks | ≈640 **(estimate; verify)** | Mg/Mn solid solution; possible primary Al₃Er nucleation; possible coherent L1₂-Al₃Er precipitation | Determine whether Er alone can replace the Zr-assisted nucleation/age-hardening route. Published strong Er alloy evidence uses Zr: measured Al–6.40Mg–0.72Mn–0.40Er–1.10Zr gave 325/438 MPa YS/UTS and 18% as built, rising to 440/520 MPa and 15.5% after 375 °C/10 h (pqac-00000051, pqac-00000052, pqac-00000054) | Strong SAASBO information value, but **no retrieved publication validates this Zr-free composition as crack-free**. Er may segregate or form coarse primary Al₃Er rather than a useful nanoscale dispersion; Mg evaporation remains important | Screen 300, 325, 350 and 375 °C; 3, 10 and 24 h. Use 375 °C/10 h only as the Zr-bearing comparator, not as a guaranteed optimum |
| 7 | Optional—highest-strength literature reproduction | Mehta Alloy F | Al–4.8Mn–0.9Cr–1.1Zr–1.2Mg; practical rounded target Al–5Mn–0.8Cr–1.1Zr–1.2Mg | **BUY:** Al–10Zr master alloy; other elements on hand | ≈680 **(estimate; verify)** | Primary Al₃Zr grain nucleation; Mn/Cr/Mg solid solution; Al₃Zr and Mn/Cr-rich precipitation | Reproduce measured-chemistry Alloy F: 390/450 MPa YS/UTS and 17% as built; 500/560 MPa and 5% after 375 °C/8 h; hardness 132→172 HV (pqac-00000024, pqac-00000040, pqac-00000047) | Best strength evidence and crack-free at 99.7–99.8% density, but aged ductility misses the 8% objective. Zr dissolution and primary Al₃Zr/sludge formation are major 350 g melt risks; add Al–10Zr early and verify complete dissolution before Mg addition | 375 °C/8 h peak-strength reproduction; also test 350 °C/8–24 h or under-ageing to trade some strength for ≥8% elongation |
| 8 | Optional—Er/Zr precipitation reproduction | Guo Alloy 3 | Al–6Mg–0.7Mn–0.4Er–1.1Zr | **BUY:** Al–10Zr master alloy; Mg, Mn and Er on hand | ≈640 **(estimate; verify)** | Mg/Mn solution strengthening; primary Al₃(Er,Zr) nucleation; Al₃Er→core–shell Al₃(Er,Zr) nanoprecipitation | Reproduce measured Al–6.40Mg–0.72Mn–0.40Er–1.10Zr: as-built 325/438 MPa YS/UTS and 18%; aged 375 °C/10 h 440/520 MPa and 15.5% (pqac-00000051, pqac-00000052, pqac-00000054) | Best documented strength–ductility balance among the optional alloys, but uses substantial Zr and Er and is sensitive to Mg evaporation. Primary particles/sludge and composition drift must be checked by ICP-OES | 375 °C/10 h; lower-temperature alternatives: 350 °C/≈25 h or 325 °C/50–100 h (pqac-00000051) |
| 9 | Optional—low-Sc bridge to Scalmalloy | Low-Sc Al–Mg–Sc–Zr | Al–4Mg–0.3Sc–0.4Zr | **BUY:** Al–10Zr master alloy; use limited Sc stock; Mg on hand | ≈640 **(estimate; verify)** | Primary Al₃(Sc,Zr) grain nucleation; Mg solid solution; coherent L1₂-Al₃(Sc,Zr) precipitation | Establish whether 0.3% Sc plus 0.4% Zr gives a useful fraction of Scalmalloy performance. Closely related literature includes Al–3.02Mg–0.2Sc–0.1Zr aged at 325 °C and reaching ≈400 MPa UTS, but the exact proposed chemistry is **not a direct reproduction** (pqac-00000039) | High probability of crack-free refinement and ageing response with much less Sc than Scalmalloy; nevertheless, 0.3% Sc may be below the threshold for fully equiaxed grains under the campaign’s coarse-powder/80 µm-spot conditions. Zr dissolution remains the main melt risk | Start 325 °C/4 h; map 300–350 °C for 2, 4, 8 and 12 h to locate peak strength while retaining ≥8% elongation |

info.query:
We must pick the first SIX aluminium alloy compositions (plus three optional extras) for a laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) alloy discovery campaign, and write a complete recipe for each. Please do a deep, quantitative literature review that lets us choose and specify them. Report MEASURED chemistries (ICP/OES of powder or part) rather than nominal ones wherever the paper gives them, and say which is which.

CONTEXT
- Goal: an alloy that is stronger than LPBF AlSi10Mg (as-built yield about 230-300 MPa) without relying on critical minerals, and/or one that approaches Scalmalloy (Al-4.6Mg-0.7Sc-0.3Zr, about 470-520 MPa yield when direct aged) with much less Sc. Strength first; ductility of at least about 8 %; relative density at least 99.5 %; crack-free.
- Powder: made in-house by 40 kHz ultrasonic atomization of 170-350 g charges melted by induction at up to about 1300 C (so far run at 810-840 C), collected under argon. Median size is coarse (D50 roughly 55-65 um), so the LPBF cut will probably be 20-63 um.
- Feedstock on hand: 6063 bar (carries about 0.5 Mg, 0.4 Si, 0.2 Fe), Al-12Si (4047) bar, Mg, Mn, Cr, Zn, Sn, Ti, Si, and small amounts of Sc and Er. Quick to buy: Fe, Cu, Ni. NOT yet on hand and uncertain: Zr (would come as Al-10Zr master alloy), Ce, Li.
- Printer: Aconity MIDI (400 W-class single-mode fibre laser, about 80 um spot), argon, build-plate heating available. Sub-size tensile bars, as-built and direct-aged.
- After the six seeds a sparse-axis-aligned-subspace Bayesian optimizer (SAASBO) picks the remaining runs over about 15 candidate elements, so the seeds should be mechanistically diverse, not six variants of one family.

QUESTIONS
1. For each family below, give the best-documented specific composition(s) and, per paper: measured composition (wt%), powder route and size, LPBF machine, laser power, scan speed, hatch, layer thickness, spot size, plate preheat, volumetric energy density, relative density, cracking observations, as-built and heat-treated yield strength / UTS / elongation (with build orientation and heat treatment), hardness, and the microstructure reported (grain size and morphology, primary and eutectic phases, precipitates, retained solute). Families:
   a. Al-Mn-Cr-Zr (Chalmers group: Mehta, Nyborg, Hryha and co-workers) and Al-Mn-Ti-Zr (Mair et al.), and Zr-free Al-Mn-Cr or Al-Mn-Mg variants.
   b. Al-Mg-Zr (Croteau, Dunand, Seidman et al.; Addalloy) and Al-Mg-Zr-Mn.
   c. Al-Fe-Zr (Constellium Aheadd CP1 type), Al-Fe-Mg-Zr (Li et al. 2025), binary Al-Fe (Qi, Takata, Kimura), Al-Fe-Cr, Al-Fe-Mn, Al-Fe-Cu, Al-Fe-Ni (AlFeNi eutectic) and Al-Fe-V-Si (8009).
   d. Al-Mg-Si eutectic-type alloys with high Mg (Al-Mg2Si pseudo-binary, Magsimal-59-like AlMg5Si2Mn, Fehrmann AlMgty, the Dreano Al-6.7Mg-3Si-1.4Ni-1Zn alloy) that print crack-free WITHOUT Zr, Sc or Ti grain refiners.
   e. Modified Al-Si-Mg: AlSi7Mg0.6 (A357), AlSi10Mg with raised Mg (1-3 wt%), with Mn, Cu, Ni, Er, Zr or Sc additions; Al-Si-Ni and Al-Si-Fe-Mn; which of these beat standard AlSi10Mg as-built or direct-aged, and by how much.
   f. Er as a Sc substitute: Al-Mg-Er-Zr, Al-Mg-Mn-Er-Zr, Al-Er-Zr, Al-Zr-Er-Yb, Al-Ni-Er-Zr (Taheri-Mousavi et al.). Is there any crack-free Er-bearing alloy WITHOUT Zr?
   g. Low-Sc Al-Mg-Sc-Zr (Sc 0.1-0.4 wt%) and low-Sc Al-Mn-Sc; the lowest Sc level that still gives equiaxed, crack-free builds and an ageing response; Sc partially replaced by Zr, Er, Ti or Y.
   h. Al-Ce(-Mg, -Mn, -Ni, -Zr), Al-Ni(-Mn, -Zr, -Sc), Al-Cu-Mn-Zr (ACMZ), Al-Cu-Mg with Ti, Zr or TiB2 (A20X, 2024+Zr), 7xxx with Zr (HRL 7A77) or with Si, and 6061 with Zr or Si.
   i. Ti as the L1_2 / D0_22 former instead of Zr: Al-Ti, Al-Mg-Ti, Al-Mn-Ti, Al-Cu-Ti, Ti-modified 2xxx/7xxx, Al-5Ti-1B (TiB2) inoculated alloys made by melt routes.
2. Zr is not yet on our shelf. Which compositions made ONLY from Al, Si, Mg, Mn, Cr, Zn, Sn, Ti, Fe, Cu, Ni, Sc and Er (no Zr, Ce, Li, Ag) have been printed crack-free by LPBF with as-built or aged yield strength above about 300 MPa? Rank them by evidence.
3. For each of the top candidates, what microstructure should we expect from OUR route (coarser 20-63 um ultrasonically atomized powder, 80 um spot, 30-50 um layers, with 25 C versus 150-200 C plate), and which features decide success (primary Al3Zr/Al3Ti nucleants at the melt-pool boundary, eutectic fraction, Mn/Cr supersaturation, Mg loss)?
4. Direct ageing (no solution treatment) schedules and expected hardening for each family, and which families lose strength on a heated plate or in stress relief.
5. Recommend a set of six seeds (2 benchmarks, 3 literature picks, 1 exploratory) and three optional extras that are (i) mechanistically diverse, (ii) makeable from the feedstock above (flag each element that must be bought), (iii) meltable and castable below about 1000 C without primary Al3Zr / Al3Ti / Al-Cr-Mn sludge in the crucible (give the liquidus where known), and (iv) each informative about a different strengthening route. State what is known and unknown for each, and which published result we would be trying to reproduce.

Give DOIs for every source and separate what the papers state from your inference.
